summaries.Q243: Put up in barely two years for the 1889 World's Fair, it marked the centenary of the Revolution and went by a name as plain as could be: "the 300-metre tower". Now the symbol of Paris, it has welcomed more than 300 million visitors since it opened.
summaries.Q19675: The largest art museum in the world, 73,000 m2 of galleries, housed in a royal residence eight centuries old. Francis I made it the emblem of the Renaissance; once Louis XIV left for Versailles, the palace slowly filled with the royal collections and became a museum in 1793. Nine departments cover Western art from the Middle Ages to 1848, plus the ancient civilisations. Pei's pyramid, opened in 1989, is the way in.
summaries.Q2981: Begun in 1163 by Bishop Maurice de Sully and finished around 1345: nearly two centuries, hence the blend of Early Gothic and Rayonnant Gothic. Between 1845 and 1867 Viollet-le-Duc restored it and slipped in motifs of his own, among them a new spire, the one carried off by the fire of 15 April 2019. It reopened on 7 December 2024.
summaries.Q23402: A station turned museum. Built by Victor Laloux between 1898 and 1900, the Gare d'Orsay escaped demolition and reopened in 1986 as a national museum. Inside, Western art from 1848 to 1914 and the largest Impressionist collection in the world: close to 1,100 canvases.
summaries.Q550: 1,910 metres in a straight line from the Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe. The avenue grew out of a vista traced by André Le Nôtre, Louis XIV's gardener, and takes its name from the Elysian Fields of Greek mythology, the resting place of virtuous souls. Crowned "the most beautiful avenue in the world", it is nonetheless shunned by Parisians.
summaries.Q193563: Heir to the royal collections gathered since the Middle Ages, it holds one of the richest bodies of material in the world: everything published in France is deposited here. The present site was inaugurated by François Mitterrand in 1995.
summaries.Q64436: Ordered by Napoleon in 1806, it was not finished until 1836, under Louis-Philippe: thirty years of building. Standing 49.5 metres high, it sits on the great Paris axis running from the Louvre pyramid to the Grande Arche at La Défense, by way of the Concorde obelisk.
summaries.Q202660: Founded by Francis I in 1530 to teach what the Sorbonne refused to touch, it has kept a rule unique in the world: every lecture is free, open to anyone, with no enrolment and no degree at the end. Its motto, Docet omnia, promises to teach all things. Some fifty chairs are created and dropped as knowledge moves on; being elected professor here remains one of the highest distinctions in France.
summaries.Q311: The most visited cemetery in the world: 3.5 million people come every year to wander among its 70,000 graves. The largest cemetery inside the city limits, it is still in use and reads as much like a wooded park as an open-air pantheon.
summaries.Q193431: Opened in 1897 as a cycling stadium, it is the oldest ground in France still in use. The present arena, by Roger Taillibert, dates from 1972 and has hosted PSG since 1974, with 48,583 seats partly perched over the ring road.
summaries.Q188190: Built in 1720 by Armand-Claude Mollet for the Count of Évreux, the mansion was paid for with the fortune of Antoine Crozat, the richest man in France, built on large-scale maritime trade and on the slave trade to Louisiana. The Regent, who had mocked this count with no Paris house of his own, came in person to hand him the promised patent. Louis XV gave it to Madame de Pompadour in 1753; it has housed the presidency since the Second Republic.
summaries.Q186115: An independent village until 1860, Montmartre has kept its country air in the middle of the city. Watched over by the Sacré-Cœur, it took in Picasso and Modigliani and still stands for a rural, bohemian Paris.
summaries.Q178065: The building that turned its architecture inside out: Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers pushed the structure, the pipes and the stairs outside to free up the floors within, and colour-coded the ducts (blue for air, green for water, yellow for electricity, red for movement). Unveiled in 1977 to the outrage of Parisians, it holds the foremost collection of modern art in Europe. Its glass caterpillar offers one of the finest views over the city.
summaries.Q187840: Charles Garnier, 35 years old and a complete unknown, won the competition launched by Napoleon III in 1861. Asked by the empress what style he was building in, he replied: the Napoleon III style. Work struck an underground water table that had to be locked into a tank, the seed of the legend of the lake beneath the Opera that Gaston Leroux would later mine. Opened in 1875, the building hides 11,000 m2 of stage and workshops behind its grand marble staircase; the Chagall ceiling dates from 1964.
summaries.Q189503: The largest square in Paris, 7.5 hectares, and the one heaviest with history: designed to carry a statue of Louis XV, it became place de la Révolution, where 1,119 people were guillotined, among them Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette. Renamed Concorde as a gesture of appeasement, in 1836 it received the Luxor Obelisk, a gift from the viceroy of Egypt and the only monument in Paris never to have switched political sides. It is 3,300 years old.
summaries.Q193582: The lower house of Parliament, 577 deputies, sitting since 1798 in the Palais Bourbon, built in 1722 for the Duchess of Bourbon, a legitimised daughter of Louis XIV. The columned front facing the Concorde is a screen added by Napoleon in 1810 to answer the Madeleine across the river: it matches nothing of the structure behind it. The chamber itself dates from 1832.
summaries.Q188856: Willed by Louis XV as a church for Saint Genevieve, the building became at the Revolution the tomb of the nation's great men. Its first occupant, Mirabeau, was thrown out a few months later: his secret dealings with the monarchy had just come to light.
summaries.Q190063: The cradle of Paris. Here the Parisii tribe settled, here Lutetia was fortified in 308, here Clovis set his capital. A chronicler in 1190 called it the head, the heart and the marrow of Paris. Its 22 hectares carry Notre-Dame, the Sainte-Chapelle and the Conciergerie, but also, at the western tip, the place Dauphine and the square du Vert-Galant, still astonishingly quiet.
summaries.Q28785: Raised after the defeat of 1870 as a "national vow", it took fifty years to build: decided in 1873, the basilica was not finished until 1923. Perched at the top of the hill, it looks out over the whole of Paris.
summaries.Q214654: The present building dates from 1885, but the institution goes back to the 1250s, when Robert de Sorbon, chaplain to Saint Louis, founded a college so that poor students of theology could live decently. Later a byword for doctrinal orthodoxy, the Sorbonne condemned Joan of Arc and had books burned before being dissolved in 1793. Richelieu's chapel, the only seventeenth-century remnant, holds his tomb.
summaries.Q1189954: Founded in 1783 by Louis XVI to train able directors for the kingdom's mines, it is the oldest mining school in France. Since 1815 it has occupied the hôtel de Vendôme on the boulevard Saint-Michel, facing the Luxembourg Gardens. Its mineralogy museum, open to the public, lines up 100,000 specimens in a nineteenth-century gallery left untouched, meteorites and giant crystals among them.
summaries.Q193193: Saint Louis had it built in seven years, between 1242 and 1248, for one purpose: to house the Crown of Thorns he had just bought from the emperor in Constantinople for more than the chapel itself cost. The architect did away with nearly every wall, leaving 1,113 stained-glass scenes across 600 m2, two-thirds of them original. The lower chapel was for the servants, the upper one for the king, who reached it straight from his palace.
summaries.Q217925: Twenty-four hectares between the Eiffel Tower and the École militaire, on a former parade ground that owes its name to the Roman god of war. Listed since 1956, the garden is part of the Banks of the Seine site on the Unesco list.
summaries.Q188977: Louis XIV had it built in 1670 to house his wounded soldiers, who until then had begged along the roads; as many as 4,000 pensioners lived here. Libéral Bruand drew the buildings, Jules Hardouin-Mansart the gold-leafed dome, one of the peaks of French classical architecture. Napoleon has lain here since 1861 in a red quartzite sarcophagus, nested like a Russian doll inside six successive coffins.
summaries.Q151030: Opened on 6 October 1889 at the foot of the Montmartre hill, on the site of the Bal de la Reine Blanche, by Joseph Oller, inventor of pari-mutuel betting, and his partner Charles Zidler. The big mill painted red, designed by Adolphe Willette, served as the sign: this was the first electrified building in Paris. The French cancan draws 600,000 spectators a year.
summaries.Q329852: Marie de' Medici, widow of Henry IV and weary of the Louvre, had a palace built from 1615 that echoed the Palazzo Pitti of her Florentine childhood, right down to the rusticated stonework of the façade. She lived there only five years before Richelieu sent her into exile. A prison under the Terror, seat of the Senate since 1799, it holds a library decorated by Delacroix. Visits are by prior booking or during the Heritage Days.
summaries.Q1538826: The world's oldest museum of technology, founded in 1794 on an idea of Abbé Grégoire's: gather the machines together and train engineers by example. It fills the former priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, whose Romanesque church makes a spectacular setting for Foucault's pendulum and Clément Ader's flying machine. Also here: Pascal's first calculating machine and Lavoisier's reconstructed laboratory.
summaries.Q309458: Laid out in 1612 for Marie de' Medici, it belongs today to the Senate and unfolds over 23 hectares of formal beds and sculpture. An international ranking in 2022 named it the most beautiful garden in Europe.
summaries.Q329948: Richelieu had this palace built in 1628 and left it to Louis XIII. In 1780 the Duke of Orléans, short of cash, ringed the garden with galleries to rent out: cafés, gambling dens, booksellers and prostitutes drew all Paris, and since the police could not set foot in a prince's home, the place became a hotbed of seditious ideas. It was here that Camille Desmoulins called the crowd to arms on 12 July 1789. Buren's striped columns arrived in 1986.
summaries.Q457318: Built for the 1900 Universal Exhibition to replace the palais de l'Industrie, it carries on its pediment the phrase that sums it up: a monument dedicated by the Republic to the glory of French art. Its nave covers 13,500 m2 under 6,000 tonnes of glass and steel, the largest glass roof in Europe. Le Corbusier proposed demolishing it in 1965; the project came to nothing, its author dying that same year. The building reopened in 2024 after restoration.
summaries.Q209626: 846 hectares west of Paris, two and a half times Central Park. A remnant of the old forest of Rouvray, this "lung" of the capital shelters the parc de Bagatelle and the jardin du Pré-Catelan.
summaries.Q1144549: Born in 1971, gone in 2018 into Sorbonne Université, it stood on the site of the abbey of Saint-Victor, which served as the city's wine market between 1813 and 1955. In 1964 Malraux handed the campus to Édouard Albert, who raised a grid of all-metal blocks inspired by the Escorial. Around the Zamansky tower runs a line by Jean Perrin: "The future is a present the past makes us."
summaries.Q377066: Under the dome on the quai de Conti sit five academies, among them the Académie française and its forty "immortals" in green coats. Created in 1795, the institution is nicknamed the "Parliament of the learned world".
summaries.Q323767: 209 metres tall, opened in 1973: for nearly forty years it was the tallest building in France, until the Tour First in 2011. Its glazed observation deck looks out over the whole city.
summaries.Q818517: The oldest and largest formal French garden in Paris, created in 1564 for Catherine de' Medici on former tile works, then redrawn by Le Nôtre in 1664 along the vista that runs all the way to the Arc de Triomphe. The palace it served burned during the Commune in 1871 and was never rebuilt. Its pools, its Maillol statues and its metal chairs make it the open-air drawing room of Parisians.
summaries.Q271639: The largest green space in Paris with 995 hectares, ahead of the bois de Boulogne. Four lakes linked by streams sit on a plateau overlooking the meeting of the Seine and the Marne.
summaries.Q330564: Eighty years of building work and as much hesitation: conceived by Napoleon in 1806 as a temple to the glory of the Grande Armée, the building nearly became the first railway station in Paris in 1837, before being consecrated as a church in 1845. Fifty-two Corinthian columns encircle it.
summaries.Q392564: Opened in 1926, it is the oldest mosque still active in mainland France. Built in Hispano-Moorish style, it raises a 33-metre minaret and can hold a thousand worshippers.
summaries.Q820892: Built by Charles Girault for the 1900 Universal Exhibition, facing the Grand Palais, it houses the fine arts museum of the City of Paris. It stands on the site of the palais de l'Industrie, pulled down in 1896.
summaries.Q272208: Opened in 1824 outside the city limits, it covers 19 hectares and holds 35,000 graves. Here lie Baudelaire, Maupassant, Sartre and Beauvoir in the same tomb, Serge Gainsbourg whose grave disappears under metro tickets and cabbages, Jean Seberg, Julio Cortázar and Samuel Beckett. A 17th-century windmill, left over from a farm, still stands inside the walls.
summaries.Q745942: The busiest station in Europe, with close to 300 million travellers a year. The present façade, finished in 1866 by Jacques Hittorff, is a railway triumphal arch: 23 statues personify the cities served, the nine largest crowning the top for international destinations, London and Brussels foremost. The iron frame of the train shed was ordered from Scotland, no French supplier being able to make it.
summaries.Q273638: Founded in 1882 by the City of Paris, on rue Vauquelin, to train engineers in physics and chemistry. Seven Nobel Prizes punctuate its history, from the Curies to Georges Charpak, and Pierre-Gilles de Gennes headed it from 1976 to 2003. Its intakes are numbered from the founding: the one that started in September 2024 was number 143.
summaries.Q28924: Six million Parisians rest in these former quarries, filled from the city's cemeteries starting in the late 18th century for reasons of public health. Twenty metres underground, 1.7 kilometres are open to visitors. The name "catacombs" is borrowed from Rome; the place was never a necropolis.
summaries.Q48756: The French space agency, created on 19 December 1961 at the instigation of Charles de Gaulle, around the Diamant launcher. On 26 November 1965 the launch of Diamant A brought France into the club of space powers; it was carried out from Hammaguir, in the Sahara, on a base that the Évian Accords left to France until 1967, three years after Algeria's independence. Its budget, 3 billion euros in 2024, is still the largest in Europe.
summaries.Q390418: The most sumptuous of the Paris bridges, opened for the 1900 Universal Exhibition. It celebrates the Franco-Russian alliance sealed in 1891: its first stone was laid in 1896 by Tsar Nicholas II in person, and it bears his father's name, Alexander III.
summaries.Q335277: The oldest bridge in Paris, despite a name that means "new bridge". Finished in the early 17th century, it was "new" in its daring: no houses on the deck, and pavements to keep pedestrians clear of the mud and the horses, a first.
summaries.Q32979361: The largest startup campus in the world: 34,000 m² installed since 2017 in the former Freyssinet railway hall, bought up by Xavier Niel.
summaries.Q61460498: Founded in 1680, it is the only national theatre with a permanent company. It is nicknamed the "House of Molière" even though the playwright had been dead seven years when it was created: his widow and his former secretary fought to keep his repertoire alive. It has occupied the salle Richelieu since 1799.
summaries.Q321621: Built over Gallo-Roman Lutetia, it has been the university heart of Paris for more than eight centuries: the university was recognised here in 1200, the collège de Sorbonne founded around 1257, and the first printing press in France opened here in 1470. Its name recalls Latin, the language of the university back then.
summaries.Q662976: Born in 1970 from the break-up of the University of Paris after May 68, it is reckoned the best law and political science faculty in the country. Its name comes from its two historic sites, the Panthéon and rue d'Assas.
summaries.Q138101: What survives of the palace of the kings of France on the Île de la Cité, from before Charles V moved out to the Louvre. The salle des Gens d'armes, a vast Gothic vessel of 1302, is the largest medieval civil hall in Europe. Later a prison, the Conciergerie saw 2 780 inmates pass through during the Terror, among them Marie Antoinette, Danton and Robespierre; most left it only for the scaffold. Its Tour de l'Horloge has carried the first public clock in Paris since 1371.
summaries.Q211034: Two cow-pasture islets joined together and built up in one go in the 17th century, which gives the island its rare unity: a grid of six streets lined with mansions raised in thirty years. Eleven hectares, 2 300 residents, no metro station, no great monument. You come for the walk along the quays and for Berthillon ice cream, made on the spot since 1954.
summaries.Q810700: A café concert in Chinese style opened on 3 February 1865, named after an Offenbach operetta. A cinema, a dance hall, then a rock venue that hosted the Velvet Underground and Prince. On 13 November 2015 an attack there killed ninety people; the hall reopened a year later, on 12 November 2016.
summaries.Q13397: Commissioned in 1983 by François Mitterrand from Ieoh Ming Pei, with no competition, it earned the president the nicknames Mitteramsès and Tontonkhamon (his name crossed with a pharaoh's) before being inaugurated in 1988, then again in 1989. Its 603 glass lozenges and 70 triangles rest on 95 tonnes of steel and 105 tonnes of aluminium. The Thinker was to sit enthroned at the centre: seen from below, he looked as if he were on a potty.
summaries.Q746647: Eleven hectares in the 18th arrondissement, the third largest cemetery in Paris after Père-Lachaise and Montparnasse. Its oddity: a road bridge, the pont Caulaincourt, literally strides over it.
summaries.Q638423: Wanted by François Mitterrand as a people's opera house to counter a Garnier judged too high society, it went in 1983 to the Uruguayan architect Carlos Ott, picked by mistake according to a stubborn legend in which the jury believed it had chosen Richard Meier. Opened on 13 July 1989 for the bicentenary of the Revolution, it lines up 2 745 seats, one of the largest opera halls in the world, and stage basements dropping 30 metres.
summaries.Q643520: In 1699 Jules Hardouin-Mansart drew the façades before knowing who would build behind them: buyers had to comply, which gives the square its flawless unity. The statue of Louis XIV was melted down during the Revolution and replaced by the Vendôme column, cast from the bronze of 1 200 cannon taken at Austerlitz. The Communards pulled it down in 1871 at Courbet's instigation; he was sentenced to pay for it, and it went back up five years later.
summaries.Q273593: The Beaux-Arts de Paris have occupied the former convent of the Petits-Augustins, on the quai Malaquais, since 1817. The site had served as a store for sculptures rescued from churches during the Revolution, and that collection of fragments embedded in the courtyard walls still gives the place its strangeness. Delacroix, Monet, Degas, Seurat and Matisse studied here. The exhibitions in the Palais des études are open to the public.
summaries.Q273518: Born in 1947 out of a section of the École pratique des hautes études, the EHESS trained and housed Braudel, Lévi-Strauss, Barthes, Bourdieu and Derrida, and made Paris the world capital of the social sciences. Its building on the boulevard Raspail is still a place of open seminars, where you can often just walk in and sit through a session.
summaries.Q1546437: Since 1968 it has occupied the former NATO headquarters, built from 1955 to 1959 by Jacques Carlu, architect of the palais de Chaillot, and laid out in the shape of an A for Atlantic Alliance. Hence an unusual way of teaching: almost no lecture theatres, but rooms carved out of the old NATO offices, knocked together three at a time.
summaries.Q778784: Here stood the fortress taken on 14 July 1789: its demolition, begun that very day, was finished exactly one year later. The square kept the name, the symbolic charge and its column topped by a gilded angel.
summaries.Q41497113: Born in 2018 from the merger of Paris-Sorbonne and Pierre-et-Marie-Curie, it brings together humanities, sciences and medicine, close to 58 000 students. Its heart beats in the Quartier latin, but it also has a campus in Abu Dhabi.
summaries.Q280413: France's largest public research body, created by decree in October 1939, on the eve of the war, to coordinate the country's laboratories. It now employs more than 30 000 people across every discipline and has produced some twenty Nobel prizes. Its headquarters occupy a building on the rue Michel-Ange, in Auteuil; its laboratories are scattered all over France.
summaries.Q857276: Housed in the east wing of the palais de Tokyo, it holds the City of Paris's modern art collection: more than 16 000 works, from Fauvism to the contemporary scene. It opened in 1961.
summaries.Q838691: Founded in 1793 by the Revolution, it took over from the royal garden of medicinal plants created in 1626, which makes it one of the oldest scientific institutions in the world devoted to the study of nature.
summaries.Q631104: Raised from 1806 to 1810 to celebrate the surrender of Ulm, it served as the ceremonial entrance to the Tuileries palace, now gone. Napoleon had it crowned with the four bronze horses stolen from Saint Mark's basilica in Venice; they were handed back in 1815 and replaced by a copy. Three times smaller than its big brother at the Étoile, it opens the perspective of the historic axis running all the way to La Défense.
summaries.Q898629: The oldest square in Paris, finished in 1612 on Henry IV's orders, on the site of the hôtel des Tournelles, which Catherine de' Medici had razed after her husband died in a tournament accident. Thirty-six identical brick and stone pavilions frame a perfectly square garden. Victor Hugo lived here for sixteen years at No. 6, now a museum. The present name rewards the Vosges département, the first to pay its taxes in 1800.
summaries.Q806950: Set up on 18 January 1800 by Bonaparte with private capital, it was nationalised only in 1946, by de Gaulle. Beneath the hôtel de Toulouse sleeps la Souterraine, an 11 000 m2 vault 26 metres down, dug from 1924 to 1927 by 1 200 workers and carried on 658 pillars. The largest strongroom in the world at the time; it holds 2 437 tonnes of gold.
summaries.Q330375: Opened in 1869 in a former bedding shop, the Folies were first called Folies Trévise. With 1 200 seats from the very first night, it is one of the oldest venues still running in Paris.
summaries.Q1327886: The largest collection of works by Claude Monet in the world, in a private mansion in the 16th arrondissement. Born from a collector's gift, it mixes Impressionism with First Empire decorative arts.
summaries.Q757180: Opened in 1849 as the gare de Strasbourg, it closes the vista of the boulevard that bears the same name. Its great glazed gable is topped by an allegorical statue of Strasbourg, joined since 1931 by one of Verdun on the matching wing added alongside. From here the soldiers of 1914 left for the Eastern front; a huge canvas by the American Albert Herter, given in memory of his son killed in action, recalls it in the concourse.
summaries.Q463055: Heir to the royal singing school of 1784 and founded in its present form in 1795, it trained Berlioz, Bizet, Debussy, Ravel and Messiaen. Long housed on the rue Bergère and then the rue de Madrid, in 1990 it moved into a building by Christian de Portzamparc at La Villette, all deconstructed volumes and rooms soundproofed from one another. Its student concerts are often free.
summaries.Q334186: Founded in the middle of the 6th century by the Merovingian king Childebert I, its first church was consecrated in 558. A royal abbey, it answered to no one but the pope, a rare privilege that made its power.
summaries.Q860172: Dug to bring drinking water into the capital and opened in 1825, it drops 25 metres through nine locks over 4.55 kilometres, from the bassin de la Villette to the port de l'Arsenal. Its swing bridges are listed.
summaries.Q640968: Seat of the city's institutions since 1357, it has watched every Paris uprising go by: Étienne Marcel, the Fronde, the Revolution, 1830, 1848, the Commune, the Liberation. Few buildings pack in so much political history.
summaries.Q743206: The national museum devoted to Picasso occupies the Hôtel Salé, one of the great Baroque mansions of the Marais, begun in 1656 for a lord of Fontenay.
summaries.Q650519: In 1911 Rodin handed his collections to the State on one condition: a museum in his name at the Hôtel Biron, where he had set up his studio alongside Matisse and Cocteau. He died in 1917 and never saw it open, two years later. It holds nearly 6,800 sculptures and 8,000 drawings, in three hectares of wooded garden.
summaries.Q1414059: Around 1773 the Duke of Chartres asked Carmontelle to compose a land of illusions in the Anglo-Chinese taste: pagoda, Dutch windmills, pyramid, feudal ruins. The Naumachia survives, its colonnade taken from a funerary monument commissioned by Catherine de' Medici. It was from this garden that Garnerin launched himself in 1797 on the first parachute jump in history.
summaries.Q1094338: It stands on the La Villette slaughterhouses, abandoned in 1974: Adrien Fainsilber kept the concrete carcass of their unfinished auction hall and filled three of its four bays. François Mitterrand opened it in March 1986, timed to the meeting of the Giotto probe with Halley's Comet. Outside, the Argonaute, a former Navy submarine, has been open to visitors since 1991.
summaries.Q295844: In the twelfth century its parish answered to the neighbouring abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Today the church commands the place Saint-Sulpice, in the Odéon quarter.
summaries.Q3075489: A glass ship signed Frank Gehry, moored in the Bois de Boulogne at the heart of the Jardin d'Acclimatation. Devoted to modern and contemporary art, it grew out of a famous rivalry between Bernard Arnault and François Pinault, who set up in Venice instead.
summaries.Q656054: Opened in 1898 on the place Vendôme by the Swiss hotelier César Ritz with the chef Auguste Escoffier, it was the first hotel in the world with a bathroom and a telephone in every room. Marcel Proust took his late-night suppers here, Hemingway drank at the bar that now bears his name, and Coco Chanel lived here for thirty-seven years.
summaries.Q167863: Willed by Jacques Chirac and drawn by Jean Nouvel, it opened in 2006 at the foot of the Eiffel Tower to show the arts of Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas. Twenty million visitors since it opened.
summaries.Q747506: The first station built in the Île-de-France, in 1837, for the Paris to Le Pecq line. Its glass and cast-iron shed fascinated the Impressionists: Monet planted his easel here in 1877 and drew twelve canvases from it, having talked the manager into stoking the locomotives with coal for extra steam. France's second busiest station, it has been a listed historic monument since 1984.
summaries.Q1329141: Paris's first metal bridge, thrown across in cast iron from 1801 to 1804 on Napoleon's orders, at a time when crossing it cost a sou. It owes its name to the Louvre, then called the Palais des Arts. Weakened by barges, it partly collapsed in 1979 and was rebuilt almost identically. Love locks brought a parapet down in 2014: every one of them was removed, and the railings replaced with glass.
summaries.Q730948: Botanical garden, menagerie and scientific campus all at once, it is the seat of the National Museum of Natural History. Glasshouses, formal French beds and exhibition galleries make it both a park and an open-air museum.
summaries.Q860994: Born from the collection of a Lyon industrialist, Émile Guimet, it opened in 1889 as the "Museum of Religions", in a building put up expressly for it. It covers the arts of the whole of Asia.
summaries.Q726781: The old orange-tree glasshouse of the Tuileries, built in 1852 and converted in 1927 to receive a gift from Monet to the State: eight Water Lilies panels in two oval rooms, under natural light, hung exactly as the painter himself dictated. He insisted that nothing break the cycle, not even a corner. The basement shows the Walter-Guillaume collection, with Renoir, Cézanne, Soutine and Modigliani.
summaries.Q218613: The largest department store in Europe and the second in the world after Macy's in New York. Thirty-seven million visitors crowd in every year.
summaries.Q13360213: Built for the 1937 World's Fair on the site of the Palais du Trocadéro, it is one of the three permanent buildings that fair left behind, with the Palais de Tokyo and the Palais d'Iéna. Its esplanade faces the Eiffel Tower.
summaries.Q537720: Opened in 1984, this convertible arena hosts the tennis Masters and the judo Grand Slam as readily as the biggest concerts. It staged the basketball and the gymnastics of the 2024 Olympic Games.
summaries.Q1613027: Thrown up in haste over the winter of 1927 to host the Davis Cup the Four Musketeers had just brought back to France, on land ceded by the Stade Français on one condition: that it carry the name of a former member, the aviator Roland Garros, killed in action in 1918. He had never played tennis. The ground now has 18 courts, among them the Philippe-Chatrier and its clay watered every evening.
summaries.Q420494: La Cipale, short for piste municipale, the municipal track, opened in 1896 in the Bois de Vincennes. An Olympic venue in 1900 and again in 1924, it hosted the finish of the Tour de France from 1968 to 1974, while the Parc des Princes was being rebuilt: this is where Eddy Merckx raised his arms. Renamed in 1987 after Jacques Anquetil, it still serves track racing and training.
summaries.Q1535247: Built for the 1937 International Exhibition and clad entirely in marble, it takes its name from the quai de Tokio that then ran along the Seine. Its west wing became a contemporary art centre in 2002, deliberately left raw, bare concrete and exposed ducting, open until midnight. The east wing houses the Musée d'Art moderne de la Ville de Paris.
summaries.Q1338207: The third largest church in Paris, behind Notre-Dame and Saint-Sulpice. Its first stone was laid on 19 August 1532, but the money kept running out: it was finished only in 1633 and consecrated in 1637, a Gothic church completed in the full flood of the Renaissance. Molière was baptised here, Louis XIV made his first communion here, Berlioz premiered his Te Deum here in 1855.
summaries.Q246448: The largest green space in Paris, 55 hectares opened in 1987 on the site of Napoleon III's slaughterhouses. Bernard Tschumi spread 26 red metal follies across a regular grid, landmarks deliberately given no fixed use. The canal de l'Ourcq runs through it, the Grande Halle of 1867 still stands, and the whole gathers the Cité des sciences, the Philharmonie and the Zénith.
summaries.Q734017: The former Gare d'Orléans, opened in 1840, whose metal shed spans 51 metres and holds a rare feature: the trains stand under a glass roof 280 metres long, still intact. From here the government fled to Bordeaux in 1914 and again in 1940. Its twin, the Gare d'Orsay, built farther downstream to bring travellers closer to the centre, became the museum everyone knows.
summaries.Q939883: Born in 1964 from the merger of the Pitié hospital and the Salpêtrière, it is today one of the largest hospitals in France.
summaries.Q1138922: Founded in 1881 by Rodolphe Salis, it was the great meeting place of le Tout-Paris and the emblem of late nineteenth-century bohemia. Erik Satie composed one of his major pieces there. The cabaret went through three successive addresses.
summaries.Q1781591: A convention centre and concert hall at the porte Maillot, on the edge of the Bois de Boulogne. The complex also takes in a hotel tower, the Hyatt Regency Paris Étoile.
summaries.Q912192: Home to the Prime Minister since 1935, this 1722 mansion long housed the aristocracy and then Talleyrand, who threw ruinously lavish parties here. It hides the largest private garden in Paris, three hectares in the middle of the 7th arrondissement, invisible from the street. In the press, Matignon means the head of government himself, a metonymy that has become automatic.
summaries.Q523312: On 9 November 1920, eight coffins exhumed from eight sectors of the front were brought together in the citadel of Verdun and shuffled several times to erase any trace of their origin. The next day Auguste Thin, aged 21, added up the digits of his regiment, the 132nd, got six, and laid his bouquet on the sixth. The flame, added in 1923, is rekindled every day at 18:30.
summaries.Q915451: The oldest music hall in Paris still in business. Joseph Oller, who had already founded the Moulin Rouge, first put up a wooden roller coaster here: the police prefect, fearing fire, made him tear it down. So he built a theatre instead.
summaries.Q175055: 3.4 hectares where seven streets and five metro lines converge, one of the biggest junctions in Paris. In the early twentieth century a cable tram set off from here to climb the hill of Belleville.
summaries.Q640447: The museum of the history of Paris, spread over two Marais mansions linked by a gallery. The sixteenth-century Hôtel Carnavalet was Madame de Sévigné's home for twenty years. The collections run from Neolithic dugout canoes recovered at Bercy to old shop signs, by way of Proust's bedroom and the cell where Louis XVI was held in the Temple. Entry to the permanent collections is free.
summaries.Q1200698: Founded in 1838, it went by the name "Au Bon Marché" for 151 years. Its present building, begun in 1869, owes its iron frame to the engineer Armand Moisant. Contrary to legend, Gustave Eiffel played only a marginal part.
summaries.Q1124095: A fifteenth-century mansion built on top of Gallo-Roman baths: facing the Sorbonne, the national museum of the Middle Ages holds one of the finest collections of medieval art in the world.
summaries.Q726531: Opened on 31 March 1913 on avenue Montaigne, it was the first concert hall built entirely of concrete, by Auguste Perret, and one of the first Art Deco buildings: reliefs by Bourdelle, a dome by Maurice Denis, 62 Lalique pieces. Less than two months later, on 29 May, the premiere of The Rite of Spring turned into a brawl.
summaries.Q1583780: Founded in 1870 by Ernest Cognacq, who sold ties on the Pont Neuf before opening a shop. The name comes from a water pump on the bridge, decorated with a figure of the Samaritan woman, that supplied the Louvre. In 1907 Frantz Jourdain gave it an Art Nouveau frame of exposed steel, dressed with wrought iron and ceramics; in 1928 Henri Sauvage added the Art Deco front on the Seine. Closed in 2005, it reopened in 2021 after sixteen years of works.
summaries.Q141747: Three kilometres driven through the city from 1802 on Napoleon's orders, and named after his 1797 victory in Italy. Its western stretch imposes unbroken arcades and identical façades, with shopkeepers forbidden to open bakeries or butcher's shops there, deemed inelegant. It runs along the Louvre and the Tuileries and belongs to the historic axis stretching from Vincennes to La Défense. Since 2020 it has been one of the capital's main cycling routes.
summaries.Q273480: Louis XV had it built in 1751, on an idea of Madame de Pompadour's, to give the sons of impoverished nobles an officer's training. Ange-Jacques Gabriel, architect of the Petit Trianon and the place de la Concorde, gave it its columned front and its four-sided dome, which closes the vista of the Champ-de-Mars. A fifteen-year-old Corsican scholarship boy passed through in 1784: Napoleon Bonaparte.
summaries.Q860166: Designed by Jean Nouvel, the building attempts a synthesis of Arab and Western culture. Decided under Giscard d'Estaing to bring France closer to the Arab countries, it was inaugurated in 1987 by François Mitterrand.
summaries.Q1133501: Opened in 1782, it saw the public premiere of The Marriage of Figaro two years later. Twice gutted by fire, in 1799 and again in 1818, this Italian-style house is today one of the six national theatres.
summaries.Q872222: The Salle Favart, third of that name on the site after two fires, including the blaze of 1887 that killed 84 people and forced France to overhaul theatre safety. The company, born in 1714 out of fairground shows, was allowed both to sing and to speak, unlike the Opéra, which held the monopoly on singing. Carmen, Manon, Lakmé and Pelléas et Mélisande all premiered here.
summaries.Q526595: The heart of the old village of Montmartre, 130 metres up, main square of the independent commune until it was annexed by Paris in 1860. Around a hundred painters set up their easels here every day, on pitches allotted by the city and so coveted that the wait can run to years. Utrillo and Picasso lived here; today it is one of the most visited places in France.
summaries.Q1996069: Housed at Les Invalides, it retraces the history of France through its wars. Born in 1905 from the merger of two military museums, it holds in particular the weapons collections of the Crown's garde-meuble and of the princes of Condé.
summaries.Q1621256: Its name commemorates the battle of the Alma, won in 1854 during the Crimean War. The bridge links the quai Branly to the avenue de New-York, at the foot of the Eiffel Tower.
summaries.Q2963665: Founded in 1896 by Charles Friedel, alarmed at how far French chemistry lagged behind its neighbours, the school passed on his death to Henri Moissan, the first Frenchman to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Closed for the first two years of the Great War, it reopened in 1916 and was among the first engineering schools to admit women.
summaries.Q48748155: Built for the 2024 Olympic Games and opened in February of that same year, this 8,000-seat convertible arena is home to Paris Basketball.
summaries.Q292258: Not an island at all but a dyke, raised in 1825 for the river port of Grenelle: 890 metres long, eleven wide, planted with trees from 1830 and run through by the allée des Cygnes. A bronze replica of the Statue of Liberty has stood watch at its downstream tip since 1889, first turned towards the Eiffel Tower so as not to turn its back on the Élysée.
summaries.Q3090513: Created in the 1850s at the initiative of a learned society, this garden was meant to "acclimatise" animals brought from all over the world. Now an amusement park, it spreads over 19 hectares on the edge of the bois de Boulogne.
summaries.Q1265070: Opened in 1882, it lines up two hundred wax figures, from Albert Einstein to Mahatma Gandhi. Its original baroque décor is intact, and its Palais des Mirages has been playing tricks on the eye for over a century.
summaries.Q1165526: A collectors' home turned museum, opened to the public in 1913. Like the Frick Collection in New York or the Wallace Collection in London, it has kept its original layout: you come as much for the mansion as for the paintings.
summaries.Q641548: A Gallo-Roman amphitheatre from the second century, able to hold 15,000 spectators, both gladiator arena and theatre stage, a rare combination. Forgotten for fifteen centuries under the fill, it resurfaced in 1869 when the rue Monge was cut through, and was saved from demolition by a campaign that Victor Hugo joined. Today people play pétanque and football there, free of charge, on the ancient tiers.
summaries.Q1092107: Moved here in 1802 for reasons of public health, then enlarged four times, it became in 1874 the aristocratic necropolis of Paris, carried by the smart districts of the Right Bank. There is a single way in, at 2 rue du Commandant-Schloesing, under an Art Deco porch from the 1930s. From the far bank of the Seine, the Eiffel Tower looks down on it.
summaries.Q1429394: The kings' parish church, right across from the Louvre colonnade, blending Romanesque, Gothic and Renaissance over eight centuries of building work. From its bell tower, on the night of 24 August 1572, rang the tocsin that gave the signal for the St Bartholomew's Day massacre. Parish of the Louvre's artists, it holds the tombs of Chardin, Boucher and Le Vau. Its five-arch porch, from the fifteenth century, is unique in Paris.
summaries.Q1431547: This 54-metre bell tower, built from 1509 to 1523 in Flamboyant Gothic, is all that survives of the church of Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie, sold off and pulled down after 1797. In 1824 an industrialist turned it into a shot tower: the drop was just long enough for molten lead to cool into round pellets on the way down. At its foot lies the first public garden square in Paris, laid out in 1856.
summaries.Q1294736: The capital's oldest hospital, founded around 650 by Bishop Landry, at first as much a pilgrims' hostel as an infirmary. For centuries, for lack of room, patients were grouped several to a bed, with no separation by illness, and the death rate was very high. Rebuilt from 1867 to 1878 as airy pavilions along hygienist lines, it now occupies the north side of the square in front of Notre-Dame.
summaries.Q1025693: For a hundred and twenty years, the chess capital of the world. Opened in 1681 near the Palais-Royal, by 1740 it was drawing every great player in Europe, starting with Philidor, the finest of his century. Diderot sets part of Rameau's Nephew here. Rousseau, Voltaire, Napoleon and, in 1844, Marx and Engels at their very first meeting all played here. The café closed in 1910; the spot today is utterly ordinary.
summaries.Q1025686: Opened in 1885, it takes its name from a statue of Flora, goddess of flowers and spring, that once stood across the boulevard. Next door to the Deux Magots, it became the heart of literary and philosophical Paris on the Left Bank.
summaries.Q174274: Founded in 1936 by Henri Langlois, it preserves more than 40,000 films. Since 2005 it has occupied a Frank Gehry building on rue de Bercy, put up in 1994 for something else entirely: the former American Center.
summaries.Q583251: A building site that ran for 133 years: begun at the chevet in 1491, it was finished only with the façade in 1624. The church crowns the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève, a step from the Panthéon, and its bell tower rises to nearly 80 metres.
summaries.Q1059546: Heir to a sixteenth-century Jesuit college renamed "collège de Louis le Grand" in 1682, it is one of the most celebrated lycées in France. The buildings you see today come from a rebuilding carried out between 1885 and 1888.
summaries.Q290355: Completed in 1905 on the site of a footbridge of 1878, it stacks a deck for pedestrians and cars under a viaduct carrying the elevated métro. Its cast-iron columns and its view towards the Eiffel Tower have made it a famous film location.
summaries.Q1503157: An English-language bookshop facing Notre-Dame since 1951, heir to a first Shakespeare and Company founded in 1919 in the Latin Quarter. Part bookshop, part antiquarian shelves, part shelter for writers passing through.
summaries.Q1469315: Built by Gabriel Davioud in 1862 for Haussmann, at the same time as the Théâtre de la Ville facing it from the other side of the square, in perfect symmetry. With 2,000 seats it was the largest house in Paris, long given over to lavish stage spectaculars. Diaghilev's Ballets Russes made their Paris debut here in 1909. The theatre hosted the César awards from 2002 to 2016.
summaries.Q684594: A triumphal arch of 1673, raised by François Blondel to the glory of Louis XIV and his Rhine campaign, on the site of a gate in the wall of Charles V. Its obelisks carved with trophies and stacked arms make it one of the models of official art under the Grand Siècle. The ramparts that framed it are gone: the arch stands alone in the middle of the crossroads, with nothing left to defend.
summaries.Q269641: Raised on the place de la Bastille between 1835 and 1840 in memory of the Trois Glorieuses, the three July days of 1830 that brought down Charles X. It rises to 50.52 m and carries at its summit the Spirit of Freedom by Auguste Dumont. For the unveiling, Berlioz conducted his Grande symphonie funèbre et triomphale while walking backwards in front of two hundred musicians.
summaries.Q143080: Four hectares on the Île de la Cité, a sixth of the island: the complex stands on the site of the palace of the kings of France, from which it has kept the Conciergerie and the Sainte-Chapelle. The present façade and the cour du Mai date from the eighteenth century, the rest from a rebuilding after the fires of the Commune. It has housed the court of appeal and the Cour de cassation since the tribunal moved out in 2018.
summaries.Q926749: Founded in 1803 in the buildings of a former Capuchin cloister designed by Brongniart, it is one of the four oldest lycées in Paris. It stands between the Gare Saint-Lazare and the boulevard Haussmann.
summaries.Q532113: Twenty-five hectares of fake mountain scenery: rocks, cliffs, a waterfall, a cave and a belvedere, carved out of old quarries. Opened in 1867 under Napoleon III, it is the work of the engineer Alphand and his landscape designers.
summaries.Q1422975: Where the great north-south and east-west axes cross, this is one of the main traffic hubs of Paris, and a stage-struck spot too, with its two theatres facing each other from either side of the square.
summaries.Q540781: It links the Eiffel Tower to the Trocadéro along the most photographed sightline in Paris. Named after a Napoleonic victory, it has belonged to pedestrians and cyclists since the 2024 Games.
summaries.Q291093: Built between 1893 and 1896, it owes its fame to Apollinaire's poem, "Under the Mirabeau Bridge flows the Seine". Listed as a historic monument since 1975.
summaries.Q1362670: The third royal square in Paris, completed in 1686, and the first conceived in a single sweep around a statue of the king, with Ionic pilastered façades imposed on every owner. The maréchal de La Feuillade ruined himself to offer it to Louis XIV. The original statue, gilded and ringed by four chained captives, was melted down during the Revolution; the one on view dates from 1822. The perfect circle now belongs to designer boutiques.
summaries.Q1111051: Forty-four metres, cast between 1806 and 1810 from the bronze of the cannon captured at Austerlitz, wrapped in a spiral of reliefs imitating Trajan's Column in Rome. The Communards brought it down on 16 May 1871 onto a bed of manure and brushwood, at the instigation of the painter Courbet, who was sentenced to pay for putting it back up and died in exile before settling the debt. It was standing again by 1875.
summaries.Q1514062: Raised to the rank of minor basilica by Pope Leo XIII in 1898, for the 14th centenary of the baptism of Clovis. It bears the name of the Frankish king's wife, Saint Clotilde.
summaries.Q1411180: Housed in a wing of the orangery of the Palais du Luxembourg, it has come under the Senate since 2000. It has no permanent collection: its calling is to host temporary exhibitions, often built around the European Renaissance.
summaries.Q644398: Built from 1787 to 1791 by Jean-Rodolphe Perronet, it changed names with every regime: pont Louis-XVI, then pont de la Révolution, pont de la Concorde from 1795, Louis-XVI again under the Restoration, then Concorde for good since 1830. Its masonry reuses stones from the demolished Bastille, "so that the people might for ever trample the old fortress underfoot".
summaries.Q656296: A real-tennis court built in 1861 in the corner of the Tuileries, by permission of Napoleon III. It became the museum of Impressionism until the collections moved to Orsay in 1986, then an art centre devoted to photography and the image. Under the Occupation it served as a sorting depot for works looted by the Nazis, which the curator Rose Valland secretly inventoried, making it possible to recover thousands of them after the war.
summaries.Q1147912: Before the café, a novelty shop sold silk lingerie here, under a sign adorned with two magots, those Chinese figurines that now sit enthroned on the central pillar of the room. The place became a café in 1884. In 1933, a group of surrealists at a terrace table, finding the Goncourt too academic, founded their own Prix des Deux Magots.
summaries.Q1878600: Housed in the buildings of the former Sainte-Geneviève abbey, of which the twelfth-century Romanesque bell tower, the Gothic refectory and the spiral staircase survive, all of it hidden behind a discreet façade on rue Clovis. Famous for its literary preparatory classes, it educated Musset, Mérimée, Sartre and Modiano. The main courtyard opens during the Heritage Days.
summaries.Q99562: Opened in 1900 to spare pilgrims the 222 steps up to the Sacré-Cœur. Turned into an inclined lift in 1991, it climbs 36 metres in under a minute and a half and carries nearly three million passengers a year.
summaries.Q946883: Created in 1995 by Dina Vierny — a Resistance fighter, gallerist and collector who was also Aristide Maillol's model — it brings together the sculptor's work and a collection of modern art. Temporary exhibitions fill out the rest of the programme.
summaries.Q1969385: Designed in 1934 to complement the menagerie of the Jardin des plantes, the “Vincennes zoo” spreads over 14.5 hectares. Its huge artificial rock, 65 metres high and a talking point from opening day, is still its signature silhouette.
summaries.Q1323635: The shortest of the Paris bridges, and one of the oldest crossing points on the Seine, it links the Île de la Cité to the Left Bank, in line with rue Saint-Jacques. The present structure dates from 1853.
summaries.Q1032646: Dug from 1802 to 1825 for a very practical reason: to give Paris the drinking water it lacked. 96.6 km as far as the Bassin de la Villette, long plied by the flûtes d'Ourcq, barges cut to fit its narrow gauge. Since the late 1990s its banks have been reshaped into a green corridor for cycling and walking.
summaries.Q1810430: Henry IV had it laid out in 1607 in honour of his son, the future Louis XIII, on ground won by joining up several islets at the tip of the Île de la Cité. A closed triangle of brick and stone houses, of which only two are original. André Breton saw in it a triangle laden with symbols; Simone Signoret and Yves Montand lived here. It is one of the quietest spots in the centre, thirty seconds from the Pont-Neuf.
summaries.Q427340: The oldest parish on the Right Bank, built over a basilica founded between 387 and 576, on a flood-free mound in the middle of the marshes. Its façade, completed around 1620, introduced a new style to France: classicism. On 29 March 1918 a German shell fired from more than a hundred kilometres away came through the roof of the nave during the Good Friday service: it was the deadliest shelling Paris suffered during the war.
summaries.Q774570: France's oldest public library: as early as 1643, Mazarin opened his personal collection to scholars one day a week, an unheard-of gesture at the time. Scattered during the Fronde and then rebuilt, it now holds 600,000 volumes in an untouched seventeenth-century room, Corinthian columns and antique busts included. Anyone can work there, on production of an ID.
summaries.Q337454: Founded in 1870 by the Italian sculptor Filippo Colarossi, this free art academy took in the students the Beaux-Arts would not admit, women included, who worked there from the live model. It closed in the 1930s.
summaries.Q751293: Founded in 1686, it is one of the oldest cafés in Paris. It opened shortly after coffee was introduced at the French court by an Ottoman ambassador, closed in 1890, then came back to life under its historic name in 1957.
summaries.Q1235554: Opened in 1893 on rue Royale, in a building that once belonged to the Duke of Richelieu, it started out as an ice-cream parlour run by an Italian family. Now one of the most famous restaurants in the world, it is Art Nouveau Paris incarnate.
summaries.Q3364319: France's second largest exhibition centre, straddling the 15th arrondissement, Issy-les-Moulineaux and Vanves. Its halls host the big Paris trade fairs, from the Motor Show to the Agriculture Show.
summaries.Q1538929: Fifteen hectares of English-style garden laid out at the end of the nineteenth century, like the Buttes-Chaumont. Its name is said to come from the mice, souris in French, drawn by the mills that once turned on the nearby Bièvre.
summaries.Q1573359: Once the place du Trône (Throne Square), renamed place du Trône-Renversé (Overturned Throne) under the Revolution before becoming place de la Nation. At its centre stands The Triumph of the Republic, a monumental bronze by Jules Dalou.
summaries.Q1329076: It links place Saint-Michel to the Île de la Cité, in line with the pont au Change. Its name comes from a vanished Saint-Michel chapel that stood inside the old royal palace.
summaries.Q517249: Henri Labrouste built it from 1843 to 1850 on a narrow plot 85 metres long, on place du Panthéon, where the collège de Montaigu once stood before becoming a hospital and then a prison. It is the first building designed specifically to house a library, heir to the collections of the abbey next door. It is open to any adult or holder of the baccalauréat.
summaries.Q1327827: It took over from the ninth-century Grand-Pont, where money changers kept shop by royal decree, hence the name. Like every medieval bridge it carried houses, pulled down in 1788. The present version dates from 1860 and bears the imperial N of Napoleon III. This is where you get the finest view of the Conciergerie and its towers.
summaries.Q895076: 2,530 metres bearing the name of the Second Empire prefect, who had to order the demolition of the house where he was born in order to open his own avenue. The work was only finished in 1926, long after his death: the boulevard then met the boulevard des Italiens, wiping out the passage de l'Opéra.
summaries.Q2060889: A planted walkway 4.5 kilometres long, laid out on a former railway line from the Bastille to the ring road. Its western stretch runs along the viaduc des Arts, some ten metres above avenue Daumesnil: it inspired New York's High Line.
summaries.Q550157: Built from 1860 to 1871 by Victor Baltard, the architect of the Paris covered markets, to keep pace with the Haussmann development of the district. Its iron frame was a daring move for a church at the time.
summaries.Q2300245: The oldest parish church in Paris after Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It replaced a Merovingian basilica dedicated to Saint Denis, five of whose capitals were reused in the present building, along with four black marble columns taken from an ancient temple. Pope Eugene III consecrated the church in 1147.
summaries.Q1683459: Nearly ten hectares of sloping gardens facing the Seine, created for the 1937 Exposition on the site of the 1878 garden. They run down from the Palais de Chaillot to the pont d'Iéna, opposite the Eiffel Tower.
summaries.Q924480: The last working windmill on the Butte, together with its brother the Radet just alongside. Between the two, the Debray family of millers opened a popular dance hall in the nineteenth century, the very one Renoir painted.
summaries.Q2307722: It takes its name from Napoleon's victory at Austerlitz in 1805. The bridge links place Valhubert, facing the Jardin des plantes, to the 12th arrondissement.
summaries.Q1146988: The embankment that follows the Seine from the pont de la Concorde to the pont de l'Alma. By metonymy the name also stands for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which sits here, next door to the palais Bourbon.
summaries.Q1027432: 2 070 metres of one of the most luxurious streets in Paris, running from rue Royale to place des Ternes. It is home to the Élysée Palace and to the windows of the great fashion houses.
summaries.Q977732: Housed since 1998 in the hôtel de Saint-Aignan, a Marais mansion of 1650 that became in the 19th century a warren of workshops lived in by Jewish craftsmen from Eastern Europe, thirteen of whom were deported. The main courtyard bears their names. The collections run from antiquity to the 20th century, with a holding of 2 700 documents on the Dreyfus affair given by the family, and canvases by Chagall, Soutine and Modigliani.
summaries.Q426974: A former piano factory turned into studios in 1889, where artists moved in from 1892 and Picasso in 1904: here he unveiled Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in 1907. Twenty-five tenants shared a single tap, hence the nickname “Lavoir” (washhouse), said to have been coined by Max Jacob out of irony. A fire gutted the place in 1970.
summaries.Q533037: 3 150 metres cut across the Left Bank, from quai Saint-Bernard to the edge of the Invalides. It is named after Germanus, bishop of Paris in the 6th century, whose abbey still stands along the boulevard.
summaries.Q1493222: Consecrated in 1861, it is the first permanent Russian Orthodox place of worship in Paris. Its gilded onion domes and Greek-cross plan signal from afar the “Russian quarter” around rue Daru.
summaries.Q586142: Built from 1861 to 1867 by Théodore Ballu where five streets meet, raised above a garden square and designed to be seen from the Opéra. At the far end of the nave, beneath the great organ, a balcony was set aside for the emperor and his retinue on great occasions: Napoleon III never came.
summaries.Q692768: Behind a façade designed by Ange-Jacques Gabriel in 1758, the mansion was built in 1775 for the duc d'Aumont, then passed to the ducs de Crillon. Seized during the Revolution, it went on to become one of the grand hotels of place de la Concorde.
summaries.Q1431541: The largest school complex in France: nearly 4 000 pupils, more than 1 300 of them in the classes préparatoires. Its buildings fill an entire block of the 16th arrondissement.
summaries.Q576507: The district takes its name from the sculptor Jean-Baptiste Pigalle. Between boulevard de Clichy and boulevard de Rochechouart, at the foot of Montmartre, it was the heart of Paris nightlife: cabarets, artists' cafés and glowing signs.
summaries.Q1469250: Its name comes from the toll once paid to cross it: a “double denier”. It links the square in front of Notre-Dame to quai de Montebello.
summaries.Q1073098: The lowest bridge in Paris. Its story begins in 1821 with a suspension bridge designed by the engineer Navier, famous for never having opened.
summaries.Q1061959: It stands on the site of one of the very first bridges in Paris. The present structure, raised in 1853 during Haussmann's works, saw its five arches cut to three in 1912, including a central metal arch spanning 60 metres.
summaries.Q1758497: The third oldest bridge in Paris, after the Pont-Neuf and the pont Marie. Listed as a historic monument, it links the Louvre's pavillon de Flore to rue du Bac.
summaries.Q1140060: Seven bridges have followed one another here since 1634; this one, all steel, dates from 1970. Closed to cars since 2014, it joins the île de la Cité to the île Saint-Louis and doubles as a stage for street musicians.
summaries.Q895078: The Boul'Mich, driven through by Haussmann in 1855 straight across the medieval tangle of the Latin Quarter, wiping out dozens of its alleys. Long the street of bookshops and student cafés, it was the scene of the barricades of May 1968, when torn-up cobblestones became missiles. It runs alongside the Luxembourg and serves the Sorbonne.
summaries.Q1854102: The former Paris stock exchange, a Greek temple of 1826 ringed by 66 Corinthian columns, ordered by Napoleon to give finance the dignity of antiquity. The corbeille, the pit where brokers shouted their orders, fell silent in 1987 with computerisation, and the exchange moved out in 1998. The building now hosts trade shows and events.
summaries.Q1250541: The oldest French institution still in business, created in 864 by an edict of Charles the Bald, and one of the oldest companies in the world. It has struck the national coinage for eleven centuries, in a neoclassical palace on quai de Conti built in 1775 by Jacques-Denis Antoine. The art workshops still work metal on site; the museum and the main courtyard are open to the public.
summaries.Q1319378: Housed since 1905 in the Louvre's Marsan wing, it still pursues its founding aim: “to keep alive in France the culture of the arts that seek beauty in the useful”. Some 150 000 objects, 6 000 of them on display, from the Middle Ages to contemporary design, with whole interiors reassembled, such as Jeanne Lanvin's apartment of 1925.
summaries.Q384602: Created in 1959, when de Gaulle advised his prime minister to carve out a ministry for André Malraux. The founding decree, written by Malraux himself, gave it the mission of making the major works of humanity accessible to as many French people as possible. People say “rue de Valois”, by metonymy, after its main address.
summaries.Q1094300: Forty houses, each tied to a country, spread over 34 hectares in the south of the 14th arrondissement: nearly 6 000 students and researchers from all over the world live here. An open-air trip around the architectural world.
summaries.Q945251: Three gardens strung together on the site of the old Bercy wine warehouses. Rails, cobbles and old storehouses survive among them, between the Accor Arena and Bercy Village.
summaries.Q3389969: A small square above the Alma tunnel, which became a place of remembrance after Diana's death in 1997. The Flame of Liberty, a replica of the one on the New York statue, has stood here since 1989.
summaries.Q1196688: Two separate bridges lined up on the axis of boulevard Henri-IV, resting on the upstream tip of the île Saint-Louis. Together they offer one of the finest views of the east end of Notre-Dame.
summaries.Q589000: It links the quai des Tuileries to the quai Voltaire, right in line with the rue des Saints-Pères, hence its other name, the pont des Saints-Pères. The first structure here dated from 1834.
summaries.Q1196667: It bears the name of Louis-Philippe I, King of the French, and joins the Right Bank to the île Saint-Louis, between the Notre-Dame and Saint-Gervais quarters.
summaries.Q670499: Opened in 1928 right next door to the Parc des Princes, it is now home to Stade français rugby. It takes its name from Jean Bouin, a distance runner killed at the front in 1914.
summaries.Q525891: Built between 1500 and 1565, in the thick of the Renaissance, yet in a deliberately old-fashioned Flamboyant Gothic. Its crypt holds the remains of the abbot Médéric, who died around 700 and whose name shrank to Merri. Its bell, cast in 1331, is the oldest in Paris. In 1832 republican insurgents dug in here behind barricades, an episode Victor Hugo recast in Les Misérables.
summaries.Q1339583: The former abbey became a military teaching hospital in 1796; in 1979 the hospital moved out into a new building raised on the old kitchen garden. It treated soldiers, but also Jacques Chirac and Nicolas Sarkozy while they were in office. Closed in 2016 to save money, the site is due to house PariSanté Campus once refurbished.
summaries.Q3279650: Headquarters of the cultural agency of the United Nations, opened in 1958 on the place de Fontenoy: a Y-shaped block on pilotis by Marcel Breuer, Pier Luigi Nervi and Bernard Zehrfuss, watched over by a committee that seated Le Corbusier and Gropius. Inside it is an open-air museum, with a Calder mobile, ceramics by Miró and a Japanese garden by Isamu Noguchi. Guided tours by prior booking.
summaries.Q1139243: A nude revue cabaret founded in 1951 by Alain Bernardin on the avenue George-V, known for its plays of light projected onto the body. Its name and its original Western decor borrowed, in the fashion of the time, from the Lakota chief Tašunka Witko, known as Crazy Horse, a figure of Native American resistance with no connection to the place.
summaries.Q751317: From 1896 to 1963, this little theatre in the cité Chaptal specialised in macabre, blood-soaked plays. Its name passed into everyday speech: anything luridly, over-the-top horrific is still called grand guignol.
summaries.Q1130784: Opened in 1854, it was built on the hygienist theories of the nineteenth century: separate pavilions linked by galleries, to slow the spread of infection. The whole complex is a listed historic monument.
summaries.Q1025695: Opened in 1898 by a café owner from the Auvergne, by the 1900s it had become the haunt of Montparnasse's foreign artists and writers, so much so that it was nicknamed the Anglo-American café.
summaries.Q547789: Balzac lived here from 1840 to 1847, in a lodge he rented under a false name to dodge his creditors. This is where he revised La Comédie humaine; the house is now one of the City of Paris museums.
summaries.Q2073308: 68 metres long and a mere 11 wide, it is one of the narrowest bridges in Paris. It skirts the apse of Notre-Dame, carrying on the line of the quai de l'Archevêché.
summaries.Q3533060: Two towers completed in 2021 at the southern tip of the 13th arrondissement. The taller one is the third highest building in Paris after the Eiffel Tower and the Tour Montparnasse, and it leans on purpose.
summaries.Q2271703: Two parabolic steel arches thrown across the water in 1903-1904 to carry the metro over the Seine, since river traffic ruled out any pier midstream. At 140 metres, it is still the longest span of any Paris bridge. Line 5 runs over it, on rails laid straight onto the structure to spare the weight of ballast.
summaries.Q2256147: Housed in the old arsenal of François I, where Sully set up in 1599 as grand master of the artillery. The library grew out of the collection of the marquis de Paulmy, sold on in 1785 to the comte d'Artois. On the day the Bastille fell, the mob came to wreck it: the Swiss porter slipped into the king's livery and the rioters, convinced they had made a mistake, turned on their heels.
summaries.Q732312: The name comes from Jehan Gobelin, a dyer famed for his scarlet reds, who set up his workshop on the banks of the Bièvre around 1447; the river and then the whole district ended up taking his name. In 1601, to stop buying tapestries abroad, Henri IV installed two Flemish weavers within these walls, Marc de Comans and François de La Planche.
summaries.Q1436962: One hundred and twenty-six metres long, one of the largest churches in Paris, built between 1653 and 1722. Its façade still carries the bullet marks of 13 Vendémiaire Year IV, when the young Bonaparte turned the cannon on the royalists massed in front of the steps. Known as the artists' parish, it holds the tombs of Corneille, Le Nôtre and Diderot.
summaries.Q549143: The oldest museum in France, direct heir to the cabinet of the kings: open to scholars from the middle of the eighteenth century, to the general public in 1791. It keeps the coins, cameos and precious objects amassed since Charles V, among them the throne of Dagobert, the great cameo of France and the Berthouville treasure. It occupies restored rooms in the Richelieu site of the Bibliothèque nationale.
summaries.Q950217: An 18-metre triumphal arch raised in 1674 to the glory of Louis XIV's victories on the Rhine and in Franche-Comté, by Pierre Bullet, a pupil of the architect of the neighbouring porte Saint-Denis. It stands where a gate of Charles V's city wall once opened. On the south face, Louis XIV poses as a half-naked Hercules, club in fist and wig on head.
summaries.Q1710383: Begun in 1824 by Jean-Baptiste Lepère and finished in 1844 by his son-in-law Hittorff, it looks out over the district from the former enclos Saint-Lazare, where Vincent de Paul died in 1660. Hittorff had part of the façade faced with enamelled lava panels: the nudity of some of the figures caused such an outcry that they were taken down as early as 1861.
summaries.Q1243760: One of the oldest churches in Paris, built around 1170, at the same time as Notre-Dame, on a place of worship going back to the sixth century. A hospice here took in pilgrims, hence the name of Julian the Hospitaller. The University of Paris held its assemblies inside until 1524, when a student riot wrecked the building. Handed to the Greek Melkite rite in 1889, it shelters an iconostasis. The little square next door keeps the oldest tree in Paris.
summaries.Q1577630: Rebuilt in the seventeenth century on the site of a thirteenth-century church, with a side doorway designed after Le Brun, who lies buried here with his mother beneath a mausoleum of his own design. It is best known for being occupied on 27 February 1977 by followers of the Society of Saint Pius X, who have never left: it has been the main traditionalist church in Paris ever since.
summaries.Q1518496: It has sat on the place Beauvau since 1861, in a mansion built in 1770 for the prince de Beauvau-Craon, which is why the ministry goes by the name of the square. A sovereign ministry, in charge of the police, the prefectures and the running of elections, it announces the results of national votes from this building. The courtyard of honour and the grand staircase open for the Heritage Days.
summaries.Q1010517: Founded in 1795 by the Convention to catch up with the English, «firmly convinced that without astronomy there was neither trade nor navy». This academy of astronomers weighed in on the adoption of the metric system and has published the Connaissance des temps since the 1797 volume. It meets every month at the Institut, on the quai de Conti.
summaries.Q1423353: The oldest cabaret in Montmartre still going, bought in 1913 by the singer Aristide Bruant. Picasso, Max Jacob and Blaise Cendrars put the world to rights here; people still sing around the table, with no microphone.
summaries.Q1187828: Here, “casino” has nothing to do with gambling: the Italian word means “little house”, and later a hall for parties. This stage on the rue de Clichy has seen the greatest names of music hall pass through.
summaries.Q1710376: A parish seat as early as the 9th century, it is one of the oldest churches on the Left Bank. Its ambulatory with twisting pillars and its charnel cloister, a rare medieval survivor, are worth the detour.
summaries.Q1338260: Founded, so tradition has it, in 1582, it passes for one of the oldest restaurants in France. Its dining room up in the air offers a panoramic view over the Seine and the apse of Notre-Dame.
summaries.Q10860702: 612 enamelled lava tiles where “I love you” is written in 250 languages, across 40 m² of the square Jehan-Rictus. Unveiled in 2000, it has become the meeting point of Montmartre lovers.
summaries.Q2296362: Gustave Moreau left his studio to the State in 1897 so that his work would stay together there. The museum holds nearly 14,000 pieces, including 850 paintings, one of the few artist's studios to have reached us intact.
summaries.Q1782606: The last apartment and studio of Eugène Delacroix, where he lived from 1857 until his death in 1863. Rescued in the 1920s by a society of the painter's friends, it became a national museum in 1971.
summaries.Q956826: A pavilion born of a bet: the Count of Artois promised Marie Antoinette he would build it in under three months. Its park, one of the four sites of the Paris botanical garden, is famous for its rose garden.
summaries.Q1418458: The first bridge in Paris made entirely of iron, 20 metres wide and crossed in a single arch. It links the Hôtel de Ville to the Île de la Cité.
summaries.Q1513866: A bridge on two levels: traffic below, and the elevated metro of line 6 running on the arches above. It links Bercy to the 13th arrondissement.
summaries.Q513655: It carries on the rue des Deux-Ponts, which crosses the Île Saint-Louis, and reaches the Left Bank. At its far end stands the statue of Saint Geneviève, patron saint of Paris, watching over the river.
summaries.Q3533204: A 180-metre skyscraper going up at the porte de Versailles, shaped like a tapering wedge. Revived in 2011, the project was held back for years by opposition from local residents and associations.
summaries.Q2051953: Fourteen hectares opened in 1992 on the site of the Citroën works at Javel, where the Traction Avant and the 2 CV rolled off the line. Gilles Clément and Allain Provost laid out a wide lawn opening onto the Seine, two monumental glasshouses and a run of serial gardens, each pairing a colour, a metal, a sense and a planet. A tethered balloon rises 150 metres above it and measures air quality.
summaries.Q2715373: The studio where Antoine Bourdelle lived and sculpted from 1885 until his death in 1929, kept exactly as it was, plasters, tools and dust included, extended by a garden of bronzes and a wing by Christian de Portzamparc. Rodin's carver for fifteen years before breaking away, Bourdelle was also Giacometti's teacher. Entry to the permanent collections is free.
summaries.Q963509: One of the oldest bridges in Paris, completed in 1635 and named after Christophe Marie, the developer who parcelled out the Île Saint-Louis. It carried fifty houses; twenty of them were swept away by a flood in 1658, along with some sixty residents. Its five arches are all different, and the niches on its piers never received the statues meant for them. Tradition says you make a wish here with your eyes closed.
summaries.Q605912: A footbridge of 1999 linking the Musée d'Orsay to the Tuileries Garden with a single 106-metre arch, without a single support in the river. Its tropical-wood deck splits into two levels that meet in the middle, letting you step straight from the lower quays to the upper ones. Renamed in 2006 after the Senegalese poet and president.
summaries.Q1809902: The largest cinema auditorium in Europe: 2,700 seats under a starry ceiling 30 metres up, opened in 1932 by Jacques Haïk, the man who had brought Charlie Chaplin to France. Its atmospheric-style decor mimics an open-air Mediterranean town. Listed in 1981, it was named the world's most beautiful cinema by Time Out in 2025, and offers a tour behind the screen.
summaries.Q1138599: The highest court of the judicial order, heir to the tribunal de cassation created in 1790. It does not retry the facts but checks that the law was correctly applied, which makes it the judge of law. It sits in the Palais de Justice on the Île de la Cité, in the gilded Second Empire grand chamber, where solemn hearings are held in red robes and ermine.
summaries.Q973216: More than 300 original works by Salvador Dalí, mostly sculptures and engravings, in a space tucked into the heart of Montmartre, on the site of the quarter's former Historial.
summaries.Q273482: Founded in 1919 by the pianist Alfred Cortot, this private conservatoire trains concert performers and teachers. Its concert hall is one of the most highly rated in Paris for its acoustics.
summaries.Q1358886: The capital's main synagogue and seat of the Chief Rabbi of Paris, it is the second largest in Europe after the one in Budapest. It was built under the Second Empire.
summaries.Q604550: Monumental glasshouses of cast iron painted turquoise blue, raised in 1898 by Jean-Camille Formigé, with a palm house and formal French gardens. It is one of the four sites of the Paris botanical garden.
summaries.Q1810868: Before it was a cabaret, the Lido was a pool with floor shows inspired by Venice, “the beach of Paris” of the 1920s. A cabaret from 1946, it put the feathers away in 2022 to reinvent itself as a musical theatre.
summaries.Q2919066: Set in the oldest house on the Butte, it also takes in the studio-apartment of Suzanne Valadon and her son Maurice Utrillo. Opened in 1960, it tells the artistic life of Montmartre from its terraced gardens.
summaries.Q950446: Perched between the Buttes-Chaumont and Père-Lachaise, this 4.5-hectare park climbs the flank of a hill. From the top the view sweeps across all of Paris, usually with fewer people than at Montmartre.
summaries.Q3378907: Opened in 2015 in the parc de la Villette, its great Pierre-Boulez hall seats 2,400 and has acoustics rated among the best in Europe. The building clad in bird scales is signed Jean Nouvel.
summaries.Q1643082: Built from 1639 to 1644 by Louis Le Vau, the future architect of Versailles, on the tip of the Île Saint-Louis, with interiors by Le Brun and Le Sueur. Voltaire lived here with the Marquise du Châtelet; the Czartoryski family then made it, in the nineteenth century, the headquarters of the Polish emigration, where Chopin, Mickiewicz and Balzac all came calling. A fire gutted it in 2013; the Hercules Gallery has been restored.
summaries.Q1374604: One of only three medieval private mansions still standing in Paris, built around 1500 for the archbishops of Sens, who held authority over Paris until 1622. Turrets, bartizans and a carriage gate give it the look of a small fortress. Queen Margot lodged here on her return from exile, at 52, with her lovers in tow; a cannonball from 1830 is still lodged in the façade. It houses the Forney library, devoted to the poster.
summaries.Q1643144: Built from 1625 to 1630 for a comptroller of finances who lost his fortune at dice and had to sell the unfinished mansion. Sully, Henry IV's adviser and by then out of favour, bought it fully fitted out in 1634, barely lived there and yet left it his name. Home to the Centre des monuments nationaux since 1967, with a discreet entrance on the place des Vosges.
summaries.Q2599177: The 280 m2 apartment Victor Hugo rented on the place des Vosges from 1832 to 1848, his most intense years: here he wrote Ruy Blas and part of Les Misérables, entertained all of Paris and learned that his daughter Léopoldine had drowned. The rooms follow his life before, during and after exile, including the Chinese salon he decorated himself for Juliette Drouet on Guernsey. Permanent collections free of charge.
summaries.Q782969: A vow of Louis XIII's, begun in 1629 and finished only in 1740: it is all that survives of the Petits Pères convent. More than thirty-seven thousand ex-votos cover its walls. Stripped of its monks during the Revolution, it housed the national lottery and then the stock exchange before being given back to worship in 1802.
summaries.Q3036228: A full-size gilded copper replica of the torch held by the Statue of Liberty in New York, given to France in 1989 by American donors in thanks for the statue's restoration. Standing at the mouth of the Alma tunnel, it spontaneously became Diana's memorial after her death on that very spot in 1997: visitors still leave messages and flowers.
summaries.Q2352779: Built by Gabriel Davioud between 1860 and 1862, to the same plan as the théâtre du Châtelet facing it. Sarah Bernhardt took over the lease in 1898 and left it her name; in 1941 the Vichy regime had it removed because she was Jewish, under its antisemitic laws. The name was given back in 1947 and has been in use again since 2023. Since the 1980s it has been one of the world's great homes of contemporary dance.
