summaries.Q917337: Behind the façade and courtyard colonnade raised from 1705 to 1709 for the Rohan-Soubise family hides a medieval mansion: the fortified gateway on the rue des Archives, with its pepper-pot turrets, was built in 1371 for the constable Olivier de Clisson and remains the only visible trace of fourteenth-century private architecture in Paris. Napoleon I installed the imperial archives here in 1808.
summaries.Q895082: Cut through market gardens after the demolition of Louis XIII's city wall, decided in 1670, it opened in 1676 as the boulevard Neuf and took the name of the Théâtre-Italien built in 1783. All through the nineteenth century this was where fashionable Paris met, at the Café Tortoni, the Café Anglais, the Maison Dorée; those addresses have given way to financial institutions.
summaries.Q1851236: Nicknamed in the nineteenth century the “boulevard du Crime”, the boulevard of Crime, for the blood-soaked melodramas staged in its many theatres. Most of them vanished when Haussmann drove his avenues through.
summaries.Q2971342: The fourth château to bear the name since the Renaissance, this one was built in the 1920s by Henri de Rothschild. It is now the headquarters of the OECD, on the edge of the bois de Boulogne.
summaries.Q1581356: The first church in France built of reinforced concrete, completed in 1904. Its technical daring earned it the nickname “Saint-Jean-des-Briques”, Saint John of the Bricks, and a listing as a historic monument.
summaries.Q1542489: Laid out in 1857 in the bois de Boulogne, on the lands of a royal abbey razed during the Revolution. It is the temple of French flat racing, host every October to the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe.
summaries.Q3152284: A leading school of fashion and luxury, founded in 1986 at the instigation of the Ministry of Industry, with Pierre Bergé as founding president. It occupies the Cité de la mode et du design, in the 13th arrondissement. Brought closer to the École de la chambre syndicale de la couture parisienne from 2019, it merged with it in 2021 and now teaches everything from the CAP vocational certificate to the doctorate.
summaries.Q1954498: Moïse de Camondo had this mansion built in the spirit of the Petit Trianon, on the edge of the parc Monceau, to house his collection of eighteenth-century French art. He left it, collections and all, to the Union centrale des arts décoratifs in memory of his son Nissim, shot down in aerial combat in 1917. Opened in December 1936, it obeys a will so precise that not a single piece of furniture was ever to move.
summaries.Q1710369: A neoclassical church of the nineteenth century that gave its name to the “lorettes”, the young women of the district who lived off the generosity of wealthy lovers. Balzac and Gavarni turned them into a literary type of romantic Paris.
summaries.Q614450: Created for the 1937 Exposition in the west wing of the Grand Palais, it brings science to life through demonstration: electrostatics, chemistry, astronomy. Generations of schoolchildren saw their first man-made lightning here.
summaries.Q645095: Opened in 1929 by Johnny Weissmuller, the future Tarzan of the screen, this Art Deco pool nicknamed “the white liner” saw the bikini shown for the first time in 1946. Left derelict and then covered in graffiti, it has reopened as a hotel and pool.
summaries.Q1810764: One of the rare points in Paris where four arrondissements meet. Busy day and night, the square marks the way into the entertainment districts of northern Paris.
summaries.Q2307584: A rail-only bridge, carrying the RER C across the Seine with a footing on the île aux Cygnes.
summaries.Q2112543: One of the oldest streets in Paris, probably traced as early as the third or fourth century. Six hundred and fifty metres of slope, markets and restaurants, which locals simply call “la Mouffe”.
summaries.Q247566: Built in 1983 on the former Pantin racecourse, this 6 800-seat hall gave its name to a whole network of venues across France. Its red frame and stretched canvas were meant to be temporary.
summaries.Q2307670: A stone bridge 168 metres long, built from 1879 to 1882 to close the wide gap between the pont de Bercy and the pont National. Five elliptical arches of unequal span. Like the district it serves, it is named after the battle where Clovis defeated the Alamanni in 496. Open views of the Bibliothèque nationale towers and the parc de Bercy.
summaries.Q281477: One of only two private cemeteries in Paris. In 1794 the bodies of 1 306 people guillotined on the place du Trône were thrown here into two mass graves, at the far end of the garden of a convent whose nuns had just been driven out. Families of the victims bought the land back to turn it into a place of remembrance. La Fayette lies under earth brought from Bunker Hill, and an American flag is renewed there every 4 July.
summaries.Q1314020: The most elegant of the Paris covered passages, opened in 1826: 176 metres under glass, floor mosaics signed by the Italian Facchina, a Pompeian decor of rosettes and goddesses. Vidocq, the former convict turned head of the Sûreté, lived at number 13. Left behind once the grands boulevards were cut through, it regained its lustre in the 1980s with antiquarian booksellers and fashion designers.
summaries.Q1572452: The collection built up by Ernest Cognacq and Marie-Louise Jay, founders of La Samaritaine, who spent thirty years buying eighteenth-century art without ever claiming to know anything about it: Fragonard, Boucher, Chardin, Watteau, Tiepolo, furniture and porcelain. It all fills the sixteenth-century hôtel de Donon, a suite of small panelled rooms that keep the scale of a private apartment. Free admission.
summaries.Q2348104: More than 200 booksellers and 900 boxcar-green boxes lined along three kilometres of quayside, on either side of the islands. The trade goes back to the sixteenth century, when pedlars hawked books on the Pont-Neuf, chased off by the licensed booksellers; in 1859 they won the right to stay put. A box is granted free of charge, but its holder must open at least four days a week. The craft is listed as intangible cultural heritage.
summaries.Q1416512: Everyone has said "Bercy" since the ministry moved there in 1988, in the 12th arrondissement. Before that it filled the Louvre's Richelieu wing, where it had fallen back after its rue de Rivoli headquarters burned during the Commune of 1871: more than a hundred years spent inside the palace.
summaries.Q1435791: The only Renaissance monument still standing in Paris, carved in 1549 by Jean Goujon for Henry II's entry into the city. It stood against the wall of the Innocents cemetery, the largest mass grave in Paris, whose two million bones were moved to the catacombs in 1786. Shifted twice, it needed a fourth carved face to stand on its own. Its marble forecourt has been a skateboarding landmark since the 1990s.
summaries.Q1766069: Founded after Clovis made Paris his capital, it held the tomb of Saint Genevieve. Its surviving buildings are now the lycée Henri-IV, and its bell tower still commands the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève.
summaries.Q590441: A Grand Boulevard lined with theatres and cafés. Here, at number 14, the Lumière brothers held the first paying public film screening in 1895.
summaries.Q1018039: A village inside the city, perched 28 metres above the Bièvre and named after Pierre Caille, who bought the hill in 1543. The Second Empire works spared this quarter, left well clear of Haussmann's rulebook. Under place Paul-Verlaine, an artesian well draws water from 582 metres at 28 degrees, feeding the pool next door since 1924.
summaries.Q1062732: Built between 1815 and 1826 on the spot where Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were first buried, along with the Swiss Guards killed in 1792. A silent memorial in the middle of a garden square, right in the 8th arrondissement.
summaries.Q1581237: Under this name, Italian commedia dell'arte troupes played in Paris from the sixteenth century, called in by Catherine and then Marie de' Medici. Their legacy fed French theatre, from Molière to Marivaux.
summaries.Q2280550: A 36-metre sphere clad in 6,433 polished steel triangles, set down in front of the Cité des sciences in 1985. Inside, a 1,000 m² hemispherical screen wraps right around the viewer.
summaries.Q910923: Against this wall in Père-Lachaise, 147 Commune fighters were shot in May 1871, at the end of Bloody Week, then thrown into a mass grave. It has become the memorial place of the French labour movement.
summaries.Q1667022: France's second museum of Asian art, born of a bequest from the banker Henri Cernuschi, who brought his collections home from a trip around the world. Its centrepiece is a monumental Buddha from Japan.
summaries.Q2597719: Housed at the headquarters of the Grand Orient de France on rue Cadet, it walks through the history of Freemasonry with aprons, swords and rare documents. It carries the "musée de France" label.
summaries.Q1726347: Thirty-five hectares in the bois de Vincennes, laid out by the landscape designer Daniel Collin on former military ground and opened in 1969 for the Third International Floralies: the largest green space created in Paris since the Second Empire. It holds 1,500 different irises, and its roofs borrow very freely from Japan, from the Yoyogi gymnasium to the Katsura villa.
summaries.Q2274186: A pedestrian bridge on a metal arch, built for the Universal Exhibition of 1900 and meant to be taken down afterwards. It still links the musée du quai Branly to the avenue de New-York.
summaries.Q2307685: A double-duty bridge, road and railway at once, at the far eastern edge of Paris. Its track carried the Petite Ceinture, the ring line now abandoned.
summaries.Q2933008: Opened in 1862 on the corner of place de l'Opéra as the café-restaurant of the Grand Hôtel de la Paix, in the purest Second Empire style. Films were already being screened here in 1896. Zola, Maupassant, Massenet and Tchaikovsky were regulars; the room and its decor have been listed as historic monuments since 1975.
summaries.Q1284688: Founded in 1984, a pioneer of corporate patronage in France, it long occupied a glass building by Jean Nouvel on boulevard Raspail, where the transparent façades doubled themselves around a cedar planted by Chateaubriand. It reopened in October 2025 on place du Palais-Royal, in a Haussmann building reworked by Nouvel with five moving floor platforms that rise and drop to reshape the space for every exhibition.
summaries.Q3268619: Founded by the educator Prosper Goubaux to prepare boys for careers in trade and industry, it moved in 1874 into the complex Eugène Train had built on boulevard des Batignolles, a hundred metres of polychrome façade bearing the words Industrie and Commerce. During the Commune, insurgents dug in on the building site; the bullet marks still show on the front.
summaries.Q1069316: Thirty-two kilometres of track looping around Paris just inside the boulevards des Maréchaux, opened section by section from 1852 to 1869 so that freight could skirt the city. Passenger traffic stopped in 1934, beaten by the métro. The line still belongs to the national rail network but sleeps under brambles, foxes and wild orchids; about ten stretches have been opened as walkways.
summaries.Q851372: Opened in 1996 near the Concorde, this bar-restaurant with its huge golden Buddha launched a fashion and a series of music compilations known the world over.
summaries.Q2626611: Built under the Second Empire to replace a chapel of 1659, it has given its name to a whole quarter of the 11th arrondissement.
summaries.Q526293: A church in the 7th arrondissement dedicated to the Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier, listed as a historic monument since 2018. It runs along the boulevard des Invalides.
summaries.Q574970: Built from the fifteenth to the eighteenth century at the foot of rue Mouffetard. In the eighteenth century its graveyard was the stage of the "convulsionaries", Jansenists in a trance whose gatherings the king ended up banning.
summaries.Q1515595: An Art Nouveau hotel of 1910, raised on boulevard Raspail at the wish of Marguerite Boucicaut to lodge the Bon Marché's customers from the provinces, just across the street. Taken over by the Abwehr in June 1940, it became in April 1945 the reception centre for returning deportees: 17,000 to 20,000 survivors passed through, their photographs pinned to election boards unused since 1936.
summaries.Q2654419: A visit beneath the cobbles, in galleries dug in the nineteenth century by the engineer Belgrand. It reveals the 2,400 kilometres of network running under the city, following in the sewermen's footsteps.
summaries.Q1632912: The City of Paris fashion museum, in a neo-Renaissance palace bequeathed by the Duchess of Galliera. Its collections hold nearly 200,000 items, among the most important in the world.
summaries.Q2707132: The longest street in Paris proper: 4,360 metres and 407 street numbers, from the Sorbonne to the porte de Versailles. It runs alongside the Jardin du Luxembourg and the Senate.
summaries.Q3176233: Three hundred metres in the heart of the Marais, the historic artery of the Jewish quarter of Paris since the Middle Ages. Bakeries, bookshops and falafel counters follow one after another.
summaries.Q3452170: 1.80 metres wide: often billed as the narrowest street in Paris, a title the sentier des Merisiers disputes. The name is said to come from an old shop sign showing a fishing cat.
summaries.Q1934495: Founded in 1855 by Jacques Offenbach, who premiered most of his operettas here. The hall, in the 2nd arrondissement, still bears the name he gave it.
summaries.Q3141829: Built in 1799, one of the oldest covered arcades in Paris along with the passage du Caire. Its name comes from the two rotundas at the entrance, where people came to gaze at panoramic canvases of Paris, Toulon, Rome or Jerusalem: they belonged to Robert Fulton, who was funding his submarine, the Nautilus, this way. Here, in 1816, the first gas lighting was attempted.
summaries.Q1488512: Two hundred years of building, from 1420 to 1620 and in five stages, for a church that stayed faithful to Flamboyant Gothic. It has no transept: in 1575 it was decided to do without one, to save time and money. Closed in 1793, it was given over to the cult of Hymen or Fidelity, then to that of Fertility, before returning to Catholic worship in 1802.
summaries.Q1567798: The oldest of the great synagogues of Paris, raised in 1822 for the Ashkenazi community expelled from the rue Sainte-Avoye; the young Offenbach conducted its choir for six months from 1833. Badly built, it was in danger of collapsing and was pulled down: the present Moorish Revival building was inaugurated in 1852 thanks to gifts from Baron James de Rothschild.
summaries.Q1247969: The Jesuit church, built from 1627 to 1641 on the orders of Louis XIII, who laid the first stone, and the first building in Paris to adopt the Roman model of the Gesù: a single nave, a façade on three levels, a 55-metre dome. The embalmed hearts of Louis XIII and Louis XIV were kept here until the Revolution. Delacroix painted a Christ on the Mount of Olives for it. Victor Hugo saw his daughter Léopoldine married here.
summaries.Q281309: Sixteen moving sculptures that spit, spin and splash in a shallow basin, made in 1983 by the couple Jean Tinguely and Niki de Saint Phalle: his the black scrap-iron machines, hers the coloured polyester figures. Every piece points to a work by Stravinsky, from The Firebird to The Rite of Spring. The basin sits on the roof of Ircam, buried under the square.
summaries.Q2714932: The house where the painter Ary Scheffer lived from 1830 to 1858, at the end of a cobbled lane in the Nouvelle Athènes district. Every Friday he welcomed Chopin, Liszt, Delacroix, Rossini and George Sand, whose jewels, hand casts and portrait the museum keeps. The rose garden and its greenhouse turned tearoom make it one of the most peaceful spots in Paris. Permanent collections free.
summaries.Q3076041: Commissioned around 1630 by Marie de' Medici from a Florentine engineer, it echoes the grottoes of the Italian gardens of her childhood. Moved in 1862, it now shelters a Polyphemus catching Acis and Galatea in each other's arms.
summaries.Q1810254: The buffet of the gare de Lyon, built by Marius Toudoire for the 1900 World's Fair and opened by President Loubet on 7 April 1901. Under eight metres of ceiling, forty-one paintings unroll the stops along the Paris-Lyon-Mediterranean line. Renamed Le Train bleu in 1963, it was saved from demolition by André Malraux three years later.
summaries.Q579087: Henry Bernard's “round house”, opened in 1963: a crown of buildings around a central tower, on the banks of the Seine. It is the home of French public radio.
summaries.Q1094332: Housed in the palais de la Porte-Dorée, built for the Colonial Exhibition of 1931 and carrying carved façades that celebrate the French empire, it tells two centuries of immigration to France. The museum takes on this colonial legacy and makes it one of the subjects of the visit.
summaries.Q2445818: A museum of postal history and stamp collecting, on the boulevard de Vaugirard since 1973. Rare stamps, mail coaches and postmen's gear retrace how letters travelled.
summaries.Q2255375: Set up in the flat where Louis Pasteur spent his last seven years, inside the institute that bears his name. The scientist rests here, in a crypt of Byzantine mosaics.
summaries.Q1853517: The 37th bridge in Paris, for pedestrians and cyclists only, thrown in 2006 between Bercy and the Bibliothèque nationale. Its lens-shaped double curve can be crossed on the upper deck or the lower one, as you like.
summaries.Q2735858: One hundred and five metres by eighty, with the fontaine Saint-Sulpice at its centre, raised by Visconti from 1843 to 1848 and adorned with statues of four great Christian preachers. It was at the Café de la Mairie, at number 8, that Georges Perec settled in for three days in October 1974 to write An Attempt at Exhausting a Place in Paris.
summaries.Q1102184: A former goods harbour turned marina in 1983, it links the canal Saint-Martin to the Seine at the foot of the Bastille. Boats wait there for the lock, between two rows of trees.
summaries.Q1470209: One thousand one hundred and fifty metres from the quai Voltaire to the rue de Sèvres. Its name comes from the ferry that carried, in the sixteenth century, the stone bound for the Tuileries building site.
summaries.Q1649419: Opened in 1927 by the Pleyel piano makers, it was long the great symphonic hall of Paris. Since 2015 and the opening of the Philharmonie, it has given itself over to contemporary popular music.
summaries.Q1643105: Built from 1655 by Antoine Le Pautre for Catherine Bellier, first chambermaid to Anne of Austria, whose standing at court rested on the queen's trust. Aware of how fragile her position was, she had four shops opened on the ground floor and drew the rents from them. The Mozarts lodged here in the winter of 1763; Wolfgang was seven.
summaries.Q1383413: The church of the Visitation, built from 1632 to 1634 to plans by François Mansart, a rotunda of 13.50 metres inspired by the Pantheon in Rome. Deconsecrated at the Revolution, it served as a book store until Bonaparte handed it to the Reformed faith in 1802. Under the east niche, in a walled vault with no inscription, the family of Nicolas Fouquet still lies.
summaries.Q2357520: Founded in 1838 by exiles from the failed 1830 uprising, on the quai d'Orléans, it became the hearth of the Polish Great Emigration and the place where a culture banned at home stayed alive. It houses the Adam Mickiewicz Museum and a Chopin room holding his death mask and a cast of his hand. Its collections are inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.
summaries.Q479218: The place of remembrance for the genocide of the Jews of France, opened in 2005 in the Marais around the tomb of the unknown Jewish martyr, raised as early as 1956. The Wall of Names carries the 76 000 Jews deported from France, among them 11 000 children; the Wall of the Righteous honours those who saved some of them. It holds the Contemporary Jewish Documentation Centre, whose archives were assembled in secret during the war. Free entry.
summaries.Q3268614: Born in 1869 as the École Monge, a private school founded by the École polytechnique graduate Aimé Godard, it moved to boulevard Malesherbes into buildings put up from 1875 to 1877 by Hector Degeorge and Gustave Eiffel. Its glazed hall, 80 metres by 30 and nicknamed la Marquise (French for a glass canopy), rests on an iron frame by Eiffel. Bought by parliament in 1894, it took the name of President Sadi Carnot, assassinated that same year.
summaries.Q279151: The third place of worship raised on the site, built from 1823 to 1830 by Étienne-Hippolyte Godde, who turned it north-south whereas the old one ran east-west. The bell tower, the only remnant of the seventeenth-century church, was worked into the new building. Its nave stands on the former graveyard, and it gave its name to the district, the boulevard and the metro station.
summaries.Q3578476: An applied-arts school for girls set up in 1864 by Élisa Lemonnier's Society for the Vocational Education of Women, first on rue Rochechouart, then rue Duperré. In 1970 it moved to rue Dupetit-Thouars, into the brick, glass and steel building of the former boys' school, keeping its original name. Fashion, textiles, ceramics and graphic design.
summaries.Q337586: Created by Louis XIV in 1671 on an idea of Colbert's, it trained generations of architects before joining the Institut de France. It sits beneath the dome on the quai de Conti.
summaries.Q810526: The largest man-made stretch of water in Paris, filled in 1808. It links the Ourcq and Saint-Denis canals to the canal Saint-Martin; its lift bridge on rue de Crimée is the last of its kind in the capital.
summaries.Q2593762: Amélie Poulain's café, at 15 rue Lepic. Ever since the 2001 film, visitors from all over the world come to sit at the counter where the heroine worked, in a setting left almost untouched.
summaries.Q23305619: Consecrated in 2016 near the pont de l'Alma, it crowns the Russian spiritual centre with its five golden onion domes. A project launched in 2007 by Patriarch Alexy II.
summaries.Q692839: Designed by Gabriel Davioud and unveiled in 1860, it has the rare distinction of filling an entire gable wall on its own. The archangel strikes the devil down above the square, now a meeting point of the Latin Quarter.
summaries.Q3145483: The main auction house in Paris, with its fifteen rooms on rue Drouot. Every afternoon you can sit in on the bidding for free, from old-master paintings to plain bric-a-brac.
summaries.Q1445889: Opened in 1927 to outshine the Dôme next door, this vast Montparnasse brasserie became the headquarters of fashionable Paris between the wars. Its thirty-two pillars were painted by artists from the neighbourhood.
summaries.Q1799101: Some sixty studios packed into a rotunda built from materials salvaged from the 1900 World's Fair. Chagall, Modigliani and Soutine lived here; artists still work here today.
summaries.Q2659603: An artificial lake in the bois de Vincennes, dug where a convent of Minim friars once stood and named after it. A car-free road runs all the way round.
summaries.Q3278824: Built between 1923 and 1925 by Le Corbusier and his cousin Pierre Jeanneret, it was the first place to apply the “five points” of modern architecture: pilotis, roof garden, open plan, ribbon window, free façade.
summaries.Q589336: Marie Curie's old laboratory, a step away from the Panthéon where she is buried. You can visit her office and the room where radioactivity was studied, still monitored for its radioactive traces.
summaries.Q1889428: Created in 1879 by Viollet-le-Duc under the name “museum of Comparative Sculpture”, it shows life-size casts of doorways, tympanums and frescoes from all over France. A cathedral of plaster inside the palais de Chaillot.
summaries.Q1286709: Housed since 1943 in the Passy wing of the palais de Chaillot, it keeps ship models, figureheads and navigation instruments. One of the oldest maritime collections in the world.
summaries.Q1787799: One thousand eight hundred and forty metres from Les Halles to the Madeleine, by way of the Palais-Royal and the place Vendôme. One of the longest streets in Paris, and one of the oldest addresses of luxury.
summaries.Q623260: An English-style garden laid out under Haussmann in the Batignolles district, with its man-made stream and its bandstand. The railway tracks out of Saint-Lazare run alongside it, down below.
summaries.Q16632474: A palace hotel opened on avenue Kléber in a 1908 building that hosted the talks on the Vietnam peace accords in 1973. Its terrace looks down on the Arc de Triomphe.
summaries.Q2426843: The highest bridge in Paris, 18 metres above the Seine, opened in 1966 in place of the viaduc d'Auteuil: three spans of 58, 93 and 58 metres carried by just two piers. From 2006 to 2012 a phone booth shaped like a flower, sculpted by Frank Gehry, was moored to it, with no purpose other than taking calls from Sophie Calle.
summaries.Q1356926: The old cardo maximus of Lutetia, nine metres wide and solidly paved, this was the road to Orléans. Its name comes from a chapel of Saint James handed in the thirteenth century to the Dominicans, known ever since as Jacobins. A ruling of 1620 forced every printer in Paris to stay within its immediate reach, on pain of death.
summaries.Q3100297: Opened in 1996 in the hôtel Hénault de Cantobre, a 1706 mansion onto which the architect Yves Lion grafted a contemporary extension, stripping out floors to create tall volumes. Wanted by Jacques Chirac when he was mayor, the MEP runs four exhibitions at once, holds 25 000 prints from the 1950s onwards and has one of the best photography bookshops in Paris.
summaries.Q3408708: The first American church built outside the United States, founded in 1814 by the American Protestants of Paris, taken in at first at the Oratoire du Louvre under Talleyrand's protection. The present building, on the quai d'Orsay, dates from 1931 and goes for a flamboyant Gothic that comes as a surprise on the banks of the Seine. Its free Sunday afternoon concerts are an institution.
summaries.Q3177458: The great pyramid's underground counterpart, unveiled in 1993: 180 tonnes of glass hung point-down above the Carrousel, with no visible structure beneath the glazing. Ieoh Ming Pei designed it to bring daylight into the shopping centre dug out under the square. Below its tip, a small stone pyramid rises to meet it and stops a few centimetres short, an encounter made famous by The Da Vinci Code.
summaries.Q1575733: Built in twenty months, from 1854 to 1856, at the request of Napoleon III in memory of his uncle Eugène de Beauharnais: it is the first church in Paris with an entirely metal structure, cast-iron columns and wrought-iron ribs. Viollet-le-Duc saw in it an "architectural lie". Jules Verne was married here in January 1857.
summaries.Q1643111: The Paris residence of the dukes of Burgundy, of which only the tour Jean-sans-Peur survives, a keep raised by the duke to assert his power in the capital. In 1548 the Confraternity of the Passion built a playhouse here: barred from staging religious plays, it won in exchange the monopoly on secular theatre in Paris, and put on Corneille, then Racine.
summaries.Q3005760: Beneath the forecourt of Notre-Dame, 1,800 m2 of remains found by chance in 1965 while a car park was being dug: a Gallo-Roman quay, hypocausts, medieval cellars, the foundations of the hospice des Enfants-Trouvés and of the rue Neuve-Notre-Dame, razed by Haussmann. Twenty centuries of city-building stacked on one spot. It is the largest urban archaeological site in Europe.
summaries.Q1131080: Founded in 1780 by Jean-Denis Cochin, parish priest of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas, who had a hospice of some forty beds built for the poor and the workers of the neighbourhood, paid for out of his own fortune and the charity of his parishioners. The present brick pavilions date from 1908-1926. It was from a room here that Jacques Chirac launched his "appel de Cochin" in 1978.
summaries.Q1629790: Chapel of the convent of the Daughters of Saint Elizabeth, founded in 1628 by Marie de' Medici and made a parish church in 1802. It holds an outstanding set of a hundred carved wooden panels of the seventeenth century, brought from an abbey in Flanders, that run all the way round the choir. Since 1938 it has been the Paris church of the Sovereign Order of Malta.
summaries.Q2942927: Consecrated in 1895, it became in 1953 the seat of the Greek Orthodox Church in France. A discreet cathedral on rue Georges-Bizet.
summaries.Q4992220: The soldiers' church, built against the Hôtel des Invalides and willed by Louis XIV to watch over his pensioners. Its nave is hung with flags taken from the enemy, and it serves as the cathedral of the armed forces diocese.
summaries.Q769842: The chapel of the Daughters of Charity on rue du Bac, where a young nun said she received in 1830 the apparitions behind the "Miraculous Medal". It is one of the busiest pilgrimage sites in Paris.
summaries.Q13408: Begun in 1928 for a fast-growing neighbourhood, it takes its cue from Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. Its concrete dome, vast and bare, comes as a surprise behind a brick façade.
summaries.Q1550337: On the hill of Auteuil, it replaced an eleventh-century church rebuilt in the fourteenth and once ringed by its graveyard. The village of Auteuil grew around it before being absorbed into Paris.
summaries.Q206656: The fourth largest church in Paris by volume: 97 metres long, a bell tower of 78 metres, an iron frame left in plain sight beneath the vaults. Built from 1863 to 1880 on a hillside, it needed a flight of 54 steps to make up the slope. On 6 May 1871, a revolutionary club meeting there called for the execution of Monsignor Darboy, archbishop of Paris, then held as a hostage; he was shot on 24 May, during the Bloody Week.
summaries.Q1285196: Built in 1906 as an annexe to a Protestant church, it has become the seat of the Serbian Orthodox Church for Western Europe.
summaries.Q2612482: Opened in 1807 as a dance hall at the foot of Montmartre, it is one of the oldest stages in Paris. Gutted by fire in 2011, it reopened in 2016.
summaries.Q1457391: An iron-and-glass nave lined with hundreds of skeletons, from rorqual whale to dinosaur. Opened in 1898, the gallery has kept its original display design: a museum of the museum.
summaries.Q3135951: Opened in 1863 in the bois de Vincennes, this is the temple of French harness racing. Its winter meeting peaks with the Prix d'Amérique, run every January before tens of thousands of spectators.
summaries.Q2059518: Built by Gabriel to house the Garde-Meuble de la Couronne, then home to the navy for two centuries. Restored and opened to the public in 2021, its loggia offers the finest view over the place de la Concorde.
summaries.Q217708: A 1928 palace hotel on avenue George-V, famous for its monumental flower arrangements, renewed every week. It belongs to a Saudi prince and is still run by Four Seasons.
summaries.Q2574917: The smallest of the four lakes in the bois de Vincennes, but the highest: its 28,000 m³ feed the whole water system of the woods by gravity alone.
summaries.Q1957702: Founded in 1794 to take in the animals of the royal menageries and of fairground showmen, it is one of the oldest zoos in the world still open. Its pavilions and aviaries are listed historic monuments.
summaries.Q2915606: A collection with no equal anywhere: scale models of the kingdom's fortified towns, begun in 1668 for Louvois, war minister to Louis XIV. These relief maps were used to plan sieges.
summaries.Q1758416: Open from 1998 to 2013 in the Chemin du Montparnasse, a dead-end lane of studios where the artists of the 1900s gathered. The villa Marie-Vassilieff keeps its memory alive.
summaries.Q2561076: Set in medieval quarries under the butte de Passy, which the friars of the Minim convent were already using as cellars in the fifteenth century: they kept a wine here that Louis XIII was fond of. Restored after 1950, the galleries served as the wine cellar of the Eiffel Tower restaurant before taking in, since 1984, two thousand tools of the vine and the wine.
summaries.Q2613771: The studio Ossip Zadkine occupied on rue d'Assas from 1928, left to the City and opened to the public in 1982, in a small house near the Luxembourg Gardens. The garden, designed by Gilles Clément, holds the sculptures inspired by forests and trees. Here blind visitors are allowed to touch the works: the artist wished it so.
summaries.Q2234305: Opened in 1960 at the porte de Versailles, its dome rests on a system invented by Buckminster Fuller. Five thousand seats for concerts and big shows.
summaries.Q1424710: Eight hectares laid out in 1985 on the site of the old Vaugirard slaughterhouses. The horse halls, the belfry and two bronze bulls remain; a plot of vines recalls the vineyard of the eighteenth century.
summaries.Q2577891: It closes off the Bassin de la Villette where it meets the canal Saint-Martin. At its centre, Ledoux's rotunda, a former toll house on the Farmers General wall, keeps watch over the locks.
summaries.Q1027719: Two hundred and eighty-two metres between the Concorde and the Madeleine, cut through in the eighteenth century. One of the grandest addresses in Paris, lined with crystal houses and luxury names.
summaries.Q2399858: Here, in the basement of the Grand Café, the Lumière brothers held the first paying film screening on 28 December 1895. Thirty-three spectators attended; the restaurant of the Hôtel Scribe occupies the spot today.
summaries.Q2711343: Founded in October 1913 by Jacques Copeau, who wanted a popular theatre free of commercialism and named it after its street so audiences could find it. Its emblem, two doves, is copied from a paving stone in the basilica of San Miniato al Monte in Florence. Threatened in 1970 by a plan for a petrol station, it is now one of the Comédie-Française's stages.
summaries.Q3527525: Built in 1913 on the model of London theatres and opened in 1919, with 1 618 seats spread over three levels. It has become the great Paris stage for musicals.
summaries.Q2000339: A glass and iron hall from 1879, built by a timber merchant who wanted to give working people a popular museum of his painting collection. His daughter sold the canvases and rented the walls to a pasta maker. The Paris centre for urban planning and architecture since 1988, it permanently displays a 40 m2 interactive model of the city, and admission is free.
summaries.Q1709616: Built from 1624 to 1726, at the same pace as the island itself, it passes for the most baroque church in Paris: gilded interior, polychrome marbles, altarpieces and chandeliers, a world away from the classical restraint of its day. Its openwork iron spire of 1765 and its clock jutting out over the street are unique in the city. It is twinned with the cathedral of Carthage, in memory of Saint Louis, who died in Tunis.
summaries.Q2379572: A rotunda 24 metres across under a dome, built from 1670 to 1676 for the convent of the Dames de l'Assomption, on rue Saint-Honoré. Charles de La Fosse painted its vault as early as 1676. Handed to the Polish Catholic Mission in 1844, it carries a bust of John Paul II on its front and hides a Polish restaurant in its crypt.
summaries.Q3145596: Opened in 1835 on rue de Rivoli by a postmaster from Calais who had grasped that the English landing in France wanted English beds, it was the first grand luxury hotel in Paris. Salvador Dalí stayed a month a year for thirty years, insisting that a herd of goats be brought into the lobby. In August 1944 the German governor von Choltitz surrendered here rather than blow up Paris.
summaries.Q691375: A rotunda of 1767, first a grain market, crowned in 1811 with the world's first iron and glass dome, a feat that sent engineers hurrying in from all over Europe. A panoramic fresco of 1889 celebrates trade between the continents, with scenes of colonial conquest that are awkward to look at today. In 2021 Tadao Ando slipped a 9 metre cylinder of raw concrete inside to hold the Pinault collection.
summaries.Q1629670: A church born in 1235 along rue Saint-Denis, rebuilt several times, then pared back in 1857 when boulevard de Sébastopol was driven through and carried off the three chapels of its apse; Victor Baltard ran the work. It keeps the relics of Saint Helena, brought in 1819 from Hautvillers Abbey by the Knights of the Holy Sepulchre.
summaries.Q2174628: The axis laid out by the Romans in the first century, later the kingdom's triumphal way: kings made their solemn entry into Paris along it, and their bodies travelled back up it toward the basilica of Saint-Denis. A street of drapers and mercers in the Middle Ages, it is one of the documented sites of prostitution in Paris since the thirteenth century. Its northern end, around the Sentier, is still the heart of the Paris textile trade.
summaries.Q2974817: A 160 metre tower of 38 floors opened in 2018 at porte de Clichy, designed by Renzo Piano as three stacked glass blocks, each narrower than the last and planted with tree-filled terraces. It brought together in one place a Paris justice system long scattered across the île de la Cité and a dozen annexes. Its 90 courtrooms make it the largest courthouse in Europe.
summaries.Q1094302: Heir to the Conservatoire's instrument cabinet, inventoried in 1793 from revolutionary seizures: of the 316 original pieces, only twelve survive. Opened in 1997 at la Villette, the museum now holds 8 419 items, 5 555 of them instruments, and shows close to a thousand. It introduced the first audio guide that lets you hear the instruments.
summaries.Q263359: Opened on 27 October 1880 by Léonard Lipp, an Alsatian from Goldbach exiled to Paris after the war of 1870, and his wife Pétronille, under the name Brasserie des Bords du Rhin. Marcelin Cazes gave it its ceramics and moleskine in 1920. The tables are ranked after Dante: paradise by the door, purgatory in the back room, hell upstairs.
summaries.Q2982896: A vast undertaking carried out from 1739 to 1745 by Edme Bouchardon on rue de Grenelle: a monumental curved façade with the City of Paris enthroned between the Seine and the Marne, framed by bas-reliefs of the four seasons. Voltaire mocked it roundly, calling it absurd to spend so much on a fountain jammed into a narrow street, with no room to step back and admire it, and yielding only two thin trickles of water.
summaries.Q3268987: Opened in 1891 by President Sadi Carnot and designed by Eugène Train, it was long the only lycée in north-east Paris and a symbol of republican schooling carried into working-class districts. Its huge courtyard and brick front make it one of the largest lycées in Paris. It has admitted girls only since 1973.
summaries.Q2638057: A real French Navy submarine, in service from 1958 to 1982, hauled up to the parc de la Villette so it could be visited. You walk its original gangways, pipes and bunks included.
summaries.Q2873657: Seven hundred and thirty metres between place de l'Alma and the Champs-Élysées, the western edge of the "golden triangle". Palace hotels and couture houses follow one another.
summaries.Q2942460: A Ukrainian Greek Catholic cathedral on rue des Saints-Pères, beside the square named after the poet Taras Shevchenko. It is the heart of the Ukrainian community in Paris.
summaries.Q1093108: Built in 1852 by Hittorff, this permanent polygonal circus first went by the name Cirque Napoléon. Bought by the Bouglione family in 1934, it still stages shows under its original timber frame.
summaries.Q1537232: A neo-Romanesque church built under the Second Empire by Émile Vaudremer for the Petit-Montrouge district. Its bell tower commands avenue du Général-Leclerc.
summaries.Q3076255: The Observatoire fountain, known as the Carpeaux fountain: four figures carrying the celestial sphere, one per continent. Bronze horses and turtles complete the scene, on the axis of the jardin du Luxembourg.
summaries.Q2915167: Built in 1923 on the site of the Count of Tolstoy's private mansion, a step from the Arc de Triomphe. Its Directoire decor gave it its name.
summaries.Q1441258: A former boulevard café turned restaurant, at the tip of Montparnasse. Hemingway wrote here, Lenin and Trotsky played chess here; copper plaques still mark the seats of its regulars.
summaries.Q2992085: Housed since 2003 in the former mansion of Marie-Laure de Noailles, redecorated by Philippe Starck, it showed the pieces of the Baccarat crystal works. The museum closed its doors for good in December 2023.
summaries.Q2024100: A brothel of the Paris of the 1930s, at 122 rue de Provence, its anglicised name a nod to the address. Behind the luxury of its themed rooms, the women who worked there were registered by the police and held to compulsory health inspections. It closed in 1946, when brothels were outlawed.
summaries.Q2739499: Ten hectares reclaimed from the old Batignolles railway yards, opened in stages since 2007. Meadows, pools and community gardens make up one of the newest parks in Paris.
summaries.Q1567455: A covered arcade from 1828 that has been the heart of Indian and Pakistani Paris since the 1970s. Restaurants, grocers and hair salons line up under its glass roof.
summaries.Q3389781: A small Montmartre square named after the singer, who lived just around the corner. Her bronze bust draws passers-by, and the view drops away over the rooftops of the Butte.
summaries.Q3449239: One of the oldest streets in Paris, once the road for wheat and for oysters coming up from Normandy. Now a pedestrian market street behind Saint-Eustache, it has kept its food shops.
summaries.Q386604: Built in 1924 on the site of a riding school, it had its first hit the very next year with Marcel Pagnol's first play, Les Marchands de gloire.
summaries.Q609842: Thrown up in just two months in 1781, it is one of the largest theatres on the Grands Boulevards, with 1 800 seats. It premiered Cyrano de Bergerac in 1897 and is still listed as a historic monument.
summaries.Q839251: A house famous above all others among architects, built from 1928 to 1931 by Pierre Chareau for Doctor Dalsace. A tenant on the top floor refused to move out, so Chareau slid the house in underneath her flat, resting it on steel columns. The façade is a wall of translucent glass blocks, and the whole interior moves: sliding partitions, retractable stairs, pivoting cupboards. It can be visited by appointment only.
summaries.Q65326: The name comes from the Italian hospitaller order of Altopascio, settled here as early as 1180 to take in pilgrims bound for Compostela, where rue Saint-Jacques left the city. The present church, built from 1630 to 1685, has a thoroughly Jansenist plainness: it was the Paris home of Jansenism, and Jean-Baptiste Denis, author of the first blood transfusion, is buried here.
summaries.Q3333162: A memorial sunk into the eastern tip of the Île de la Cité, inaugurated in 1962. A narrow staircase leads down to a closed courtyard open to the Seine through a grille: the river is in sight, the way out is not. The crypt lines up 200 000 glass rods, one for each person deported from France. Georges-Henri Pingusson designed every proportion to produce physical oppression.
summaries.Q775591: The largest artists' residency in the world: 310 live-in studios between the Marais and Montmartre, a thousand creators a year. The idea came from a speech by the Finnish artist Eero Snellman at the 1937 Exposition, taken up after the war by Félix and Simone Brunau, two Resistance members; the Cité opened in 1965. Its studios are open every Wednesday evening.
summaries.Q2901309: The first library in the world devoted to the history of women, founded in 1932 by the journalist Marguerite Durand, who gave her collection to the City of Paris in her lifetime. A former actress turned editor of La Fronde, the 1897 daily written, typeset and printed entirely by women, she had kept everything: letters from Louise Michel, manuscripts by Colette, suffragist posters. Free to consult.
summaries.Q1452637: An indoor riding school built in 1721 to train the young Louis XV, and from 1789 to 1798 the chamber where the Revolution's assemblies sat. A committee of six deputies, Guillotin among them, had toured more than twenty buildings before settling on this long hall of 51 metres. Louis XVI was tried here; in 1798 the Assembly moved on to the palais Bourbon.
summaries.Q569075: Begun in 1635 by François Mansart for the secretary of state de La Vrillière, with a gallery of 40 metres hung with canvases by Poussin, Guido Reni and Pietro da Cortona. The comte de Toulouse, Louis XIV's legitimised son, had Robert de Cotte redo it in rocaille panelling and mirrors. Under the Revolution it served as a paper store, which is what saved it; the Banque de France has sat here since 1810.
summaries.Q2756450: Haussmann laid it out in 1858 to open up the view of Garnier's future opera house, funnelling seven streets towards a single vanishing point. He imposed uniform, restrained façades on the surrounding buildings so that nothing would rival the palace. The café de la Paix has held one corner since 1862. It is one of the busiest crossroads in Paris, where three metro lines meet.
summaries.Q373890: Driven out of the Palais-Royal because her success was overshadowing the Comédie-Française, Mlle Montansier won Napoleon's backing at 77 and had this theatre built; it opened on 24 June 1807. Offenbach premiered La Belle Hélène here in 1864, and it is where Zola has Nana make her debut. Façade and lobby are classified, the auditorium listed, since 1974.
summaries.Q1581988: The name comes from the Servants of the Virgin Mary, settled here in 1258, in a black robe and a white cloak. The present church dates from 1685-1690, but its façade is borrowed: built in 1705 for Saint-Éloi-des-Barnabites, on the Île de la Cité, it was re-erected here by Baltard in 1863. The Bavarian pulpit of 1749 is inlaid with wood, pewter, ivory and mother-of-pearl.
summaries.Q376490: The name has covered three successive theatres. The first, opened in 1634 on rue Vieille-du-Temple by the actor Montdory, broke the monopoly of the hôtel de Bourgogne and premiered Corneille's Le Cid in 1637, a triumph that set off a literary quarrel lasting several years. The second dates from 1791, the third from 1976 on rue Volta, where the present company keeps up the classical repertoire.
summaries.Q1030135: It all starts in 1872 with a modest chapel paid for out of rector Maurice d'Hulst's own pocket; too cramped, it gave way in 1898 to Brother Gérard Grunblatt's neo-Gothic building. Raised to the rank of minor basilica by Paul VI in 1966, it is hemmed in by the surrounding block and easy to miss from the pavement of boulevard de Ménilmontant.
summaries.Q2669368: Roman baths built at the turn of the first and second centuries, at the corner of the cardo and the decumanus of Lutetia. The frigidarium is the only room to have kept its original roof: its groin vault peaks at 14.50 metres, one of the highest still standing in the Roman West. Blue pigment has recently been found on the vault, and red ochre on the walls.
summaries.Q3280855: A terraced garden opened in 1928 facing Notre-Dame, on the site of an annexe of the Hôtel-Dieu. It holds the oldest tree in Paris, a black locust planted in 1601 by the botanist Jean Robin, now hollow, leaning and propped up on a concrete crutch, but still flowering. Fragments of Notre-Dame are laid out along the paths.
summaries.Q888776: An open-air dance hall opened in 1873 on rue de la Gaîté, which borrowed its name from a nineteenth-century puppeteer clown before becoming one of the capital's great music halls. Joséphine Baker made her last stage appearance here: the day after the fourteenth performance, on 10 April 1975, she suffered a stroke and died on the 12th.
summaries.Q3076336: Two twin fountains set up in 1840 by Jacques Hittorff on either side of the obelisk, the fontaine des Mers to the south and the fontaine des Fleuves to the north, modelled on those of St Peter's Square in Rome. Their purpose was political: to take over a square where the memory of the guillotine was still unbearable, by filling it with water, gilded bronze and colour.
summaries.Q3076281: Commissioned by Napoleon in 1806 to give Parisians free drinking water while trumpeting his victories, whose names are carved into the column: Lodi, Arcole, Rivoli, the Pyramids, Marengo, Austerlitz, Jena. A gilded Victory with outspread wings crowns it. In 1858 it was shifted twelve metres without being taken apart, slid along rails in one piece.
summaries.Q656302: Founded in 1059 and handed over to the monks of Cluny in 1079, it became the richest Parisian holding of the Burgundian abbey, with its fortified wall and its yearly fair. Its ambulatory choir, from around 1135, ranks among the very first experiments in Gothic architecture. The monks' refectory, a masterpiece by Pierre de Montreuil, now serves as the Conservatoire's library; the church holds Foucault's pendulum.
summaries.Q3491901: The church of the village of Clignancourt, swallowed up by Paris in 1860. It fills an entire block facing the town hall of the 18th arrondissement, on place Jules-Joffrin.
summaries.Q3498663: Begun in 1858 on the land of La Chapelle, before the village had even been annexed to Paris, and consecrated in 1861. In the heart of the Goutte-d'Or, it has remained a landmark of the neighbourhood.
summaries.Q3495995: Built along the Estrée, one of the oldest roads in Paris, laid out by the Romans. Tradition has it that Saint Genevieve had a first shrine to Saint Denis raised on this spot.
summaries.Q1153474: The first church in Roman Baroque style built in Paris, at the beginning of the 17th century for the Discalced Carmelites. Its vaults hold the remains of the victims of the September Massacres of 1792.
summaries.Q1629067: Built on the Roman road linking Senlis to Orléans, it blends Flamboyant Gothic with a 19th-century façade. Its fair, the foire Saint-Laurent, was one of the largest in Paris.
summaries.Q1076211: Built at the end of the 18th century in the shape of a Roman basilica, it gave its name to the Roule district. You will find it on rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré.
summaries.Q3585089: Begun in 1933 at the porte de Saint-Cloud, in a Romanesque-Byzantine style. Its 65-metre campanile towers over the whole south-west of Paris.
summaries.Q1165249: The official residence of the President of the National Assembly, right next door to the Palais Bourbon. Built in the 18th century, it has kept its state rooms and its garden overlooking the Seine.
summaries.Q3145551: A palace hotel on rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré, named in tribute to a much-travelled English earl of the 18th century. Its inner garden of 1,200 m² is one of the largest in the capital.
summaries.Q1263082: A hanging garden of 3.5 hectares laid over the deck that covers the tracks of Montparnasse station. Stairways lead up to it straight from the station: few Parisians even suspect it is there.
summaries.Q2090916: Created in 1949 to keep alive the memory of a people in diaspora, it traces 3,000 years of Armenian history through 1,200 works, some of which have been shown at the Louvre.
summaries.Q2023566: A space devoted to the arts of Africa, the Caribbean and their diasporas, opened in 1986 and closed in 2017. Its name paid tribute to a Dutch humanist of the 17th century.
summaries.Q2449709: Founded in 1951 by the Union des fabricants in a mansion of the 16th arrondissement, it sets genuine objects against their copies: handbags, watches, medicines, spare parts. A lesson in vigilance, in pictures.
summaries.Q3055415: Two rooms where Édith Piaf lived in 1933, turned into a museum by an association of the singer's friends. You visit by appointment, as if calling on someone at home.
summaries.Q3329213: Housed in an 18th-century mansion, it showed the work of the painter Ernest Hébert, bequeathed to the State in 1978 by his heir.
summaries.Q2985016: What is left of the Togo and Cameroon pavilions from the 1931 Colonial Exhibition, now the seat of the Union bouddhiste de France. It shelters the tallest Buddha in Europe and relics given by Thailand.
summaries.Q2055773: A covered arcade from 1845, the first built entirely of metal and glass. It houses the musée Grévin, a hotel and curiosity shops, running between the boulevard Montmartre and the rue de la Grange-Batelière.
summaries.Q3377183: The residence of the President of the Senate since 1825, tucked against the Palais du Luxembourg. Marie de' Medici lived here while her great palace next door was being finished.
summaries.Q3390667: In front of the Panthéon, between the Sainte-Geneviève library and the town hall of the 5th arrondissement. It was one of the very few squares in Paris with no greenery at all, until it was redesigned in 2018.
summaries.Q2976283: The embankment that runs along the Seine at the foot of the Eiffel Tower, from the pont de l'Alma to the passerelle Debilly. It gave its name to the museum of indigenous arts standing beside it.
summaries.Q3448845: The cobbled street climbing towards the top of the butte, one of the most painted in Montmartre, notably by Utrillo. Van Gogh lived at number 54, and Amélie Poulain's café is at number 15.
summaries.Q496060: The only building in Paris signed by Oscar Niemeyer, designed in 1965: a rippling glass façade and a half-buried white dome sheltering the Central Committee hall. A masterpiece of modern concrete, on place du Colonel-Fabien.
summaries.Q3527666: Opened in 1822 as the "théâtre Montmartre", it is one of the oldest stages in Paris. In the 1920s Charles Dullin turned it into a home of avant-garde theatre; the square outside now bears his name.
summaries.Q3527480: Licensed in 1838 on the boulevard des Batignolles, then a separate town founded eight years earlier, it opened as the théâtre des Batignolles, then became the théâtre des Arts in 1907. It took its final name only in 1940, under the direction of Jacques Hébertot. Camus premiered Caligula here in 1945, with Gérard Philipe and Michel Bouquet.
summaries.Q3527516: Born in 1848 from a show booth on the carré Marigny, it has become one of the most elegant venues in Paris, on the corner of the Champs-Élysées. Its two theatres hide behind a screen of greenery.
summaries.Q12432989: A flying angel-demon carved from twenty tonnes of stone by Jacob Epstein between 1911 and 1914, paid for by an admirer. Long covered in lipstick kisses, the tomb is now shielded behind glass.
summaries.Q2942526: Cathedral of the Armenian Apostolic Church, built between 1902 and 1904 thanks to the patronage of an Armenian oil magnate. It is the heart of the Armenian community in Paris.
summaries.Q3058455: A vast green carpet laid out in the early eighteenth century to show off the northern front of the Invalides. It runs all the way down to the Seine and the pont Alexandre-III.
summaries.Q3076272: A specimen of the Egyptian revival craze that followed Bonaparte's Egyptian campaign. The statue passes for a fellah, but is thought to portray Antinous, the favourite of the emperor Hadrian.
summaries.Q2010697: The old cattle hall of the slaughterhouses, built from 1865 to 1867 by Jules de Mérindol, a pupil of Baltard, and the only one of the three livestock halls still standing on its original spot. 245 metres long, 85 wide, 19 high: it held 1,360 head of cattle on opening day, and up to 5,000 before the market closed in 1974.
summaries.Q3135866: France's benchmark course for jump racing, tucked away in the Bois de Boulogne. Every spring its hedges and banks host the Grand Steeple-Chase de Paris.
summaries.Q3145892: A nineteenth-century mansion next door to the Élysée, owned by the State. It puts up foreign heads of state on official visits.
summaries.Q3162304: A discreet garden on the rue de Babylone, once a convent's kitchen garden. Vines, fruit trees and lawns make it one of the most peaceful corners of the 7th arrondissement.
summaries.Q636136: Laid out in 1977 on the grounds of the former Villemin military hospital, this canalside garden owes its existence to a plan abandoned: the site had been earmarked for a motorway interchange. Its name pays tribute to Mahsa Jîna Amini, the young Iranian woman who died in 2022 after her arrest by the Tehran morality police. Since 2005 it has been home to Le Poireau agile, the first community garden created inside a public park of the City of Paris.
summaries.Q677543: The gardens flanking the lower Champs-Élysées, between the Concorde and the rond-point. Groves, theatres and pavilions make up an old-style promenade, laid out in the nineteenth century.
summaries.Q2659121: Twelve hectares of water at the heart of the Bois de Vincennes, with two islands linked by bridges. On the île de Reuilly, an artificial grotto and waterfall crowned by a romantic rotunda by Gabriel Davioud.
summaries.Q384109: A natural pond of one and a half hectares on the edge of Saint-Mandé, ringed by an English-style garden. The most intimate of the four lakes of the Bois de Vincennes.
summaries.Q2744339: A curved glass front on the quays, opened in 1997 to make Japanese culture better known. On the top floor, a genuine pavilion where you can follow the tea ceremony.
summaries.Q3323344: Set up on the Champ-de-Mars in 1989 for the bicentenary of the Revolution, this monument by Ivan Theimer and Michel Jantzen takes its cue from Egyptian mastabas. Two bronze obelisks carry the Declaration of 1789 amid a swarm of symbols; look for the statue of the woman and child, the little one wears a hat made of newspaper.
summaries.Q3329915: Housed in the hôtel de Salm, facing the musée d'Orsay, it brings together French and foreign decorations, medals and orders of chivalry. Napoleon made this palace the seat of his new order.
summaries.Q3364132: Four hectares in the middle of the Chinatown of the 13th, opened in 1937. Sports pitches, playgrounds and old trees make it the lungs of the neighbourhood.
summaries.Q3363846: A terraced park pressed up against the ring road, in the south of the 13th. It is named after Marshal Kellermann, the victor of Valmy.
summaries.Q1678564: A covered arcade rebuilt in 1997 near the gare Saint-Lazare, on the site of a nineteenth-century passage. Its glass roof now shelters a shopping centre.
summaries.Q1563864: A small round square at the top of the rue Mouffetard, where the four quarters of the 5th meet. Its café terraces and its fountain make it one of the liveliest spots in the Latin Quarter.
summaries.Q3390544: Opened in 1801 by a decree signed by Bonaparte, it took its present name in 1932 in memory of the Battle of the Pyramids. Its gilded statue of Joan of Arc makes it a landmark facing the Tuileries.
summaries.Q2375304: A grand hotel on the avenue Montaigne, opened in 1913 and unmistakable with its red awnings and geraniums. Christian Dior set up his fashion house right across the street; Paris modelling has kept the habit ever since.
summaries.Q3447379: Two hundred and thirty-six metres in the old Saint-Paul quarter. The street runs alongside the lycée Charlemagne and one of the few remnants of Philippe Auguste's city wall still on view.
summaries.Q3447571: Opened in 1865, this cobbled street of painted house fronts is one of the most photographed in Paris. Superstition of the day: there is no number 13, replaced by an 11 bis.
summaries.Q3451781: Five metres seventy-five: the shortest street in Paris is really nothing but a stairway of fourteen steps linking rue de Cléry to rue Beauregard.
summaries.Q3451827: Recorded as early as the fourteenth century, this Marais street takes its name from the almshouses that sheltered the destitute here, exempt from taxes. It runs from place des Vosges into the heart of the quarter.
summaries.Q2292251: Born in 1893 out of Lugné-Poe's company, this theatre premiered Jarry's Ubu Roi in 1896, one of the loudest scandals in the history of French theatre.
summaries.Q366980: Its origins go back to a performance space the Duke of Richelieu had built for himself around 1730. Today's house, on rue Blanche, also holds the smaller salle Réjane.
summaries.Q744459: Opened in 1876, then left to rot, the theatre was rescued in 1974 by Peter Brook, who chose to keep its peeling walls. That ruined look became its signature the world over.
summaries.Q3527526: It descends from a theatre licence granted in 1817 to Pierre-Jacques Seveste for the suburbs: the district would not join Paris until 1860. The present house, opened in 1886, is the work of Charles Peigniet, an architect who had also worked on the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty in New York.
summaries.Q3533192: A residential tower in the 13th arrondissement, with a private indoor pool and a solarium reached from the 34th floor. A manifesto for the vertical Paris of the 1970s.
summaries.Q749491: The arches of an old nineteenth-century railway viaduct, turned into craft workshops. The coulée verte runs along the top; below, cabinetmakers, violin makers and restorers work behind the glass fronts.
summaries.Q2859718: Twelve hectares in the bois de Vincennes, nearly 1 400 trees and 885 taxa, around a school of arboriculture founded in 1867 under Haussmann and moved here in 1936. The first plantings date from 1939; the war interrupted them in favour of food crops, and they resumed only after 1946.
summaries.Q2956582: Raised on the exact spot of the Bazar de la Charité, where a fire killed 126 people in 1897, most of them women of the aristocracy. The chapel is their memorial.
summaries.Q959018: A church in the 15th arrondissement dedicated to Our Lady of La Salette, grown out of an earlier chapel in the neighbourhood. Its concrete nave dates from the rebuilding of the 1960s.
summaries.Q3492201: It gave its name to a whole quarter of the 6th arrondissement. That name recalls that in Gallo-Roman times this area was still nothing but fields outside the walls.
summaries.Q123149: A church of iron and rivets, finished in 1902 for the working-class district of Plaisance. Its exposed metal frame, borrowed from industrial market halls, pays tribute to the world of labour: unique in Paris.
summaries.Q3581820: A large Jesuit chapel built from 1855 to 1858 on rue de Sèvres, dedicated to the founder of the Society of Jesus. Its neo-Gothic nave hides behind a discreet façade, almost invisible from the street.
summaries.Q3581916: One of the first neo-Gothic churches in Paris, built from 1854 to 1859 by Jean-Baptiste Lassus: it was his last project and, they say, his finest work. Its two bell towers carry spires 57 metres high. From 1891 to 1924, the Belleville funicular stopped at its foot.
summaries.Q3583582: The parish of Chaillot goes back to the eleventh century. The present church, on avenue Marceau, was rebuilt in the 1930s in a neo-Romanesque style of very clean lines.
summaries.Q3583589: Built on rue Saint-Dominique in the Gros-Caillou quarter, whose name is said to come from a big boundary stone that served as a landmark out in the fields. Behind its classical front waits a luminous nave.
summaries.Q669574: Raised at the turn of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries where rue de Tolbiac meets rue Bobillot, just as the Butte-aux-Cailles quarter was filling up with people.
summaries.Q3076130: Also known as the fontaine Trogneux, it comes from the eighteenth-century scheme to bring water to the faubourg Saint-Antoine. Listed as a historic monument, it still stands guard on the corner of rue de Charonne.
summaries.Q13859872: Built from 1718 to 1720 by Jean-Baptiste Leroux for the Marquis d'Avaray, it stayed two centuries in his family before being sold to the Netherlands in 1920. An embassy until 1973, it has been the ambassador's residence ever since. Its first occupant was Horace Walpole, the man we owe the notion of serendipity to.
summaries.Q3145768: Built in the 1720s on rue Saint-Dominique, it was the home of Letizia Bonaparte, Napoleon's mother. It has housed the office of the Minister for the Armed Forces ever since.
summaries.Q3146282: Built between 1770 and 1776 for the Duke du Châtelet, it served in turn as the school of Ponts et Chaussées, an imperial residence, an Ottoman embassy, then the archbishop's palace of Paris.
summaries.Q1643072: A neo-Renaissance château right in the middle of the city, built in the 1880s for the banker Émile Gaillard, who wanted a setting worthy of his medieval collection. Since 2019 it has housed the Cité de l'Économie.
summaries.Q3152461: Founded in 1906 by Albert I of Monaco, the oceanographer prince, to spread the sciences of the sea. Its wooden lecture hall and marine frescoes have never been touched up.
summaries.Q3191872: A Tibetan Buddhist temple opened in 1985 in the bois de Vincennes, next door to the Grande Pagode. Its frescoes and prayer flags take the walker somewhere else entirely.
summaries.Q6455598: Alain Passard's restaurant on rue de Varenne, three Michelin stars since 1996. The chef caused a stir in 2001 by striking red meat off the menu to devote himself to the vegetables of his own kitchen gardens.
summaries.Q3207410: A café-concert built in 1887 in Pigalle, on the site of the La Boule Noire dance hall, where audiences came to cheer Mistinguett, Maurice Chevalier or Arletty. Turned into a cinema for B movies and kung-fu films in the 1940s, the hall reopened in 1987 with Les Rita Mitsouko, redecorated by Philippe Starck.
summaries.Q722496: Built in 1896 by the architect Alexandre Marcel, at the height of the craze for Japan, it was a gift from the director of Le Bon Marché to his wife. The very year it opened, she left her husband and kept La Pagode after their separation. A cinema since 1931, it has been closed since 2015 and is due to reopen in late 2026.
summaries.Q3227400: A brothel opened in 1931 on boulevard Edgar-Quinet, in the neo-Egyptian decor that made its reputation. Like other establishments of the kind, it rested on the prostitution of women subject to police registration and to compulsory health inspections. It closed in 1946, when brothels were outlawed.
summaries.Q367569: A café-théâtre founded in 1974 in the back room of a Montparnasse bistro. This is where the gang of Jugnot, Balasko, Clavier and Lhermitte created the shows that would become Le Père Noël est une ordure and Les Bronzés.
summaries.Q1998638: The museum of the Paris hospitals, long housed in the hôtel de Miramion on quai de la Tournelle. It keeps the memory of eight centuries of public assistance, from the Hôtel-Dieu to the modern hospitals.
summaries.Q2920606: At the Invalides, it retraces the history of the order created by de Gaulle in 1940 to honour the Compagnons de la Libération. Belongings of resistance fighters, deportees and soldiers of the Free French Forces.
summaries.Q2796641: Two hectares of contemporary sculpture, free to wander, along the Seine between the Jardin des Plantes and the Institut du Monde Arabe. The jardin Tino-Rossi also hosts riverside dances in the warm months.
summaries.Q4820646: A perfume museum set in a private mansion near the Opéra, where you follow the perfumer's craft step by step, from the organ of essences to the copper stills.
summaries.Q1955698: The mansion was never Henner's: built in 1876-1878, it was the home and studio of the painter Guillaume Dubufe, at whose table Henner dined three times. In 1921 Marie Henner, widow of the artist's nephew, bought it from Dubufe's heirs and gave it to the State in 1923. The Egyptian mashrabiyas of the red studio are still in place.
summaries.Q3364196: A terraced park clinging to the hillside, right beside the ring road in the 19th arrondissement. Laid out in the 1930s, it opens from its summit onto a clear view to the north-east.
summaries.Q899223: A private collection of merry-go-rounds, fairground organs and carnival games from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, housed in the old Bercy wine warehouses. A theme park of the past, still in working order.
summaries.Q3390301: Its name comes from the estrapade, a military punishment carried out on the spot: the condemned man was hauled up on a rope, then dropped into empty air. Today it is one of the quietest squares in the 5th arrondissement.
summaries.Q21098117: A quadrilateral caught inside boulevard Saint-Germain, ringed by pedestrian crossings, straight across from Les Deux Magots, where the two philosophers were daily regulars. The name was voted in March 2000 and the square inaugurated on 11 April by Jean Tiberi. Sartre lived a few steps away, at 42 rue Bonaparte.
summaries.Q3389906: It covers the eastern half of the former Cimetière des Innocents, the main burial ground of Paris from the Middle Ages to the eighteenth century, whose bones were carted off to the catacombs in 1786. A market grew up around the Fontaine des Innocents, then a garden square in 1860, replaced by today's place in 1973.
summaries.Q65155752: The crossroads where rue Dauphine, rue de Buci, rue Mazarine, rue de l'Ancienne-Comédie and rue Saint-André-des-Arts all meet, a step from Odéon. In 2018 the Conseil de Paris gave it the names of the painter Louise Catherine Breslau and of the writer and designer Madeleine Zillhardt.
summaries.Q493084: One of the oldest arteries in Paris, running from the Bastille to Nation. It was the street of the cabinetmakers and the cradle of popular revolt: the rioters of 1789 and of 1848 set out from here.
summaries.Q739347: Opened in 1202 across the old Garlande estate, it has kept its medieval look: a curving line, narrow pavements, cobbles and timber-framed houses. At number 42, a relief of Saint Julien le Pauvre already recorded in 1380 is set into the front of a cinema that has been screening The Rocky Horror Picture Show since 1975.
summaries.Q2174633: Eight hundred and fifty-five metres through the heart of the Marais, along the road that led, as early as the thirteenth century, to the Temple enclosure. Private mansions and hidden courtyards follow one another.
summaries.Q3469861: A thousand-seat concert hall built in 1907 by the Gaveau piano firm, devoted to chamber music and the recital. Its acoustics make it one of pianists' favourite halls.
summaries.Q528218: An 1863 garden square enclosed by railings designed by Davioud, in the 9th arrondissement. Its tall trees and its playground make it a breath of air between the boulevards.
summaries.Q1130752: One of the last monumental synagogues in Paris, built in the style born in the nineteenth century with the emancipation of France's Jews. It serves the Grenelle district.
summaries.Q3527699: Opened in 1868 on rue de la Gaîté, it was put together from materials salvaged from a theatre of the 1867 Universal Exhibition. A pocket-sized Italian-style house, still in business.
summaries.Q121635: Opened in 1820 to give beginner actors somewhere to perform, hence its name: a gymnasium for the stage. The licence granted came with an odd rule: repertoire plays had to be boiled down, works in several acts reduced to one act, one-act works to a single scene. Marie Bell ran it from 1962 until her death in 1985; it was renamed after her.
summaries.Q392352: The weeping Muse of Music, carved by Auguste Clésinger and unveiled in 1850. Chopin lies here, but his heart stayed in Warsaw, sealed inside a pillar of the Church of the Holy Cross.
summaries.Q2864808: An auction house set in a private mansion on the rond-point des Champs-Élysées. Classic cars, comic art and contemporary works all go under the hammer here.
summaries.Q47686171: Jeff Koons's bouquet, given to Paris after the 2015 and 2016 attacks and installed near the Petit Palais. Its funding and its location made plenty of ink flow before it was unveiled.
summaries.Q2968411: A château completed in 1725 for the Duchess of Orléans, on the heights of Charonne. Demolished at the end of the 18th century, it survives only in a few street names and one pavilion in the 20th arrondissement.
summaries.Q2962563: One hundred and thirty metres of white concrete raised in 1970-1971 to vent the fumes of a district heating plant, taller than the second level of the Eiffel Tower. The city would have nothing with an industrial air about it, so the chimney was designed by a sculptor, François Stahly. Since 2011 a pair of peregrine falcons has nested at the top.
summaries.Q3000918: A cobbled street lined with former wine warehouses now turned into shops and restaurants. The rails of the railway that once brought in the barrels still run between the stones.
summaries.Q41355013: The first Carmel in Paris, founded in 1603 on rue Saint-Jacques, facing the Val-de-Grâce: it became the order's mother house in France and drew the highest nobility. Louise de La Vallière, the first favourite of Louis XIV, entered in 1676 and spent the rest of her life there. Suppressed at the Revolution, then re-established as early as 1800, it saw its buildings pulled down in 1900 and disappeared for good in 1906.
summaries.Q3126070: A Baltard iron-and-glass hall at the foot of Montmartre, in turn a market, a school and a municipal garage, now a museum of art brut and naive art. Under its glass roof there is also a bookshop and a café.
summaries.Q3145924: An 18th-century mansion on rue de Grenelle, now the residence of the prefect of Paris and Île-de-France. Its garden is one of the largest in the faubourg Saint-Germain.
summaries.Q3145495: The hotel grew up around the Fouquet's, the brasserie opened in 1898 by restaurateur Louis Fouquet on the corner of the Champs-Élysées. For a century its red terrace has been the haunt of the film world.
summaries.Q577871: The former colonial trial garden, laid out at the end of the 19th century east of the bois de Vincennes to acclimatise crops from the colonies. In 1907 it hosted a colonial exhibition for which “villages” were built, where people from the colonies were put on display before the Parisian public. Its derelict pavilions, overrun by vegetation, still bear the traces of it.
summaries.Q3162654: Opened in May 2007 at 45, rue d'Aubervilliers, this park of more than 42 000 m² came out of a campaign by local residents, associations and elected officials, to a design by the landscape architect Michel Corajoud. It occupies the cour du Maroc, a freight yard left idle since the 1990 years; of the railway, only the two entrance pavilions remain.
summaries.Q3220192: The most monumental version of Brancusi's Kiss, set on a grave in the Montparnasse cemetery. Two bodies cut from a single block of stone, barely roughed out: a radical break with the sculpture of its day.
summaries.Q614681: A cabaret opened on 10 January 1922 by Louis Moysés on rue Boissy-d'Anglas, the lair of Cocteau and of fashionable Paris in the Roaring Twenties. Its name comes from Darius Milhaud's ballet, not the other way round, whatever Paris believes. Jazz musicians came to play here once their own gigs were over, which is why the French still call a jam session a bœuf. Since 1941 it has stood at 34, rue du Colisée.
summaries.Q3237914: A philosophy bookshop and publishing house founded in 1911 on the place de la Sorbonne. Generations of students have bought their Kant and their Descartes here; the shopfront has never changed.
summaries.Q3240129: A little train on a fifty-centimetre gauge, opened in 1878, running the 800 metres from the porte Maillot to the Jardin d'acclimatation. It is the first very narrow gauge line in France.
summaries.Q6737052: The flat where Auguste Comte, the founder of positivism, lived from 1841 until his death in 1857. Furniture, library and papers have stayed exactly where they were: a 19th-century philosopher's home left intact.
summaries.Q29645460: A five-star hotel set in a former Belle Époque brothel near Pigalle. The decor plays the shady Paris of 1900 to the hilt, boudoirs and velvet included.
summaries.Q3323414: A gift from Poland to France: Antoine Bourdelle's column to the poet Adam Mickiewicz, commissioned in 1908, sketched in 1909 and unveiled only twenty years later, on the place de l'Alma, on 28 April 1929, a few months before the sculptor's death. Motor traffic had it moved to the cours Albert-Ier in 1956.
summaries.Q3329119: The garden-level flat where Georges Clemenceau lived from 1896 until his death in 1929, kept exactly as it was. His hat and his ankle boots are still waiting by the door.
summaries.Q7700501: The tennis museum, inside the Roland-Garros grounds. Rackets, trophies and film archives retrace the history of the French Open.
summaries.Q3361034: Built in 1861 on the quai Branly to house the imperial stables, it now holds offices of the Presidency of the Republic and official apartments.
summaries.Q3361114: An 1876 hall on rue du Faubourg-du-Temple, long devoted to the café-concert and later to the one-man show. Its five hundred seats have witnessed many a comedian's first night.
summaries.Q3363264: Opened in 1889, this is the oldest cabaret still running in Paris. Its iron framework is said to be the work of Gustave Eiffel, in a Latin Quarter hall hidden behind an unremarkable façade.
summaries.Q20203644: The banks of the Seine handed back to walkers and cyclists on both sides of the river, right in the centre. Deckchairs, floating gardens and open-air bars have taken over from the riverside expressway.
summaries.Q3368175: A private covered arcade in the 2nd arrondissement, running between rue Saint-Denis and boulevard de Sébastopol. One of the most discreet in the old arcade district.
summaries.Q3471001: An exhibition space run by Eau de Paris, devoted to water's journey to the tap: the springs, aqueducts, reservoirs and underground network beneath the capital.
summaries.Q3389720: By metonymy, “Beauvau” means the Interior Ministry, housed in the hôtel of the same name. The square opens onto the rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré, a stone's throw from the Élysée.
summaries.Q3390237: A circular square designed by the Catalan architect Ricardo Bofill and ringed with postmodern colonnades. At its centre stood, for many years, a huge sloping fountain, le Creuset du temps.
summaries.Q14629277: A small square in the quartier de l'Europe, where every street is named after a capital city. This is where Gustave Caillebotte painted Paris Street; Rainy Day.
summaries.Q3390375: Two hundred and eighteen metres by one hundred and twenty-eight, wrapped around a church built like a Greek temple. Delicatessens and luxury houses make it one of the tastiest squares in Paris.
summaries.Q3390541: A busy crossroads between the Étoile and the Batignolles, where the avenue de Wagram comes out. Its flower market is one of the last left in the capital.
summaries.Q3390656: A horseshoe-shaped square bordering the Palais Bourbon to the south, extending its courtyard. One of the most harmonious ensembles in the faubourg Saint-Germain.
summaries.Q3389996: A square in the 14th arrondissement named in tribute to the young Tunisian whose self-immolation, in December 2010, set off the Arab Spring.
summaries.Q3451646: Nine hundred metres through the Marais, past the grand mansions that became the National Archives and gave the street its name.
summaries.Q3451893: A pedestrian street in the Halles district, named after the Italian bankers who settled there in the Middle Ages. Today it packs in central Paris's jazz clubs.
summaries.Q3449203: A decree of 1859 opened this twenty-metre-wide street to double, on a gentle slope, the historic line of the narrow rue Mouffetard and rue Descartes; it took the name of the mathematician Gaspard Monge in 1864.
