Cutting it through shaved off the flank of the montagne Sainte-Geneviève: the rue Rollin, sliced clean, now ends in a staircase. Works in 1869 uncovered the Arènes de Lutèce.
summaries.Q3449238: Nine hundred and thirty-nine metres running north from the Halles: the old road to the village of Montmartre, long before the boulevard cut across it.
summaries.Q3449997: Opened in 1633 and named after Anne of Austria, it also went by “rue au Sang”, blood street. A hub of gay Paris from the late 1960s to the 1980s, it was nicknamed the “rue des mecs”, the guys' street; Japanese restaurants then took over and made it, in the 2000s, the heart of the Japanese quarter.
summaries.Q2430641: A theatre that has changed address several times since 1827, specialising in vaudeville and comedy. The current house stands on the boulevard Poissonnière.
summaries.Q3498678: The Jussieu tower, heart of the Sorbonne University campus, named after a former dean. Its terrace offers a rare panorama over the whole south of Paris.
summaries.Q3538873: A court like no other: its judges are business people elected by their peers, sitting in threes to settle disputes between companies and run insolvency proceedings. Heir to the consular courts, the first of which appeared in Lyon in 1419, the Paris one was set up by an edict of 1563; the name commercial court dates from 1790.
summaries.Q17511676: The largest English-language library in continental Europe, founded in 1920 with the books sent to American soldiers of the Great War. Hemingway and Gertrude Stein were members.
summaries.Q2870499: At 119, rue Saint-Lazare, a brasserie opened in 1892 whose façade was redone two years later by Paul Marbeau for an Alsatian restaurateur: brick and half-timbering, a stork on the chimney, and Gambrinus, king of beer, enthroned in the middle. Listed as a historic monument in 1997, it has housed a McDonald's since 1998.
summaries.Q2365441: A former Irish lightship, moored opposite the Bibliothèque nationale and turned into a concert venue in 1999. Three hundred people danced in its red hull, below the waterline.
summaries.Q2896969: A cobbled street lined with listed former wine warehouses, converted into shops and restaurants in 2000. The rails of the train that brought the barrels still show between the cobbles.
summaries.Q4465808: Founded in 1875 under the patronage of Ivan Turgenev for the Russian exiles of Paris. Looted by the Nazis in 1940, it has patiently rebuilt its Russian-language collections.
summaries.Q28946738: The chapel of the Foreign Missions Seminary, built in 1683 on the rue du Bac. Its crypt holds the relics of missionaries sent to evangelise Asia, many of whom never came back.
summaries.Q3001383: A tree-lined promenade created by Marie de' Medici along the Seine, from the Concorde to the place du Canada. This was where the court took its carriage rides in the seventeenth century.
summaries.Q3580345: The church of the village of Bercy, now stranded on a traffic island in the middle of the cars. It recalls the days when wine barrels were loaded here.
summaries.Q3076205: Built in 1846 at 70, rue de la Roquette, this half-domed fountain was fed by the canal de l'Ourcq to slake the then very crowded faubourg Saint-Antoine. A bronze lion mascaron spat a steady trickle of water and the date can still be read in Roman numerals at the back of the vault; it runs dry today.
summaries.Q3076264: The lions of place Félix-Éboué, a work by Gabriel Davioud. The fountain was moved here when place de la République was redesigned.
summaries.Q3076267: The Nubian lions guarding the entrance to the parc de la Villette. Engineer Girard's fountain first stood on place de la République before being taken apart and rebuilt here.
summaries.Q945052: A former reservoir turned into a fountain on place Jean-Baptiste-Clément, where rue Lepic meets rue Norvins. It recalls the days when the hill had to pump up its own water.
summaries.Q3076063: Erected in 1715 at the expense of Anne of Bavaria, Princess Palatine, it backed onto the outbuildings of her mansion at 12 rue Garancière. Once those were gone, it was rebuilt on its original spot, in front of the block put up in 1913. A discreet insert in the wall, a bronze lion mascaron: a commercial fountain, beside which eight water carriers' barrels stood parked at night.
summaries.Q3078275: A nineteenth-century military fort in the northern part of the bois de Vincennes, quite separate from the château next door. The army still has services based there.
summaries.Q1995733: Seven hundred and seventy thousand specimens, including a room of giant crystals brought from around the world. The gallery in the Jardin des Plantes also keeps the gems of the French crown.
summaries.Q3145705: Built in 1681 by the master mason Tape for Jacques Laugeois d'Imbercourt, a wealthy farmer-general, this mansion at 15 rue de l'Université housed the offices of the Revue des deux Mondes from 1883 to 1988. Bought in 1881 by the surgeon Alfred Richet, it sheltered four generations of Richets. Listed as a historic monument in 1996.
summaries.Q1440242: The mansion of the Master of the Horse of France, built around 1676 and then rebuilt by Robert de Cotte. It was pulled down around 1806 to clear the approaches to the Louvre.
summaries.Q3145789: A late seventeenth-century mansion, heavily reworked in the nineteenth for the Duke of Castries. It stands on rue de Varenne, among the great houses of the faubourg Saint-Germain.
summaries.Q3145797: Built in the 1720s on rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré, it was Pauline Bonaparte's home before being sold to the Duke of Wellington in 1814. It has been the British ambassador's residence ever since.
summaries.Q19904532: Built in 1772 by Brongniart for the Marquise de Montesson, the Duke of Orléans's secret wife. It covered a vast stretch of the Chaussée-d'Antin, since carved up into building plots.
summaries.Q3145934: A neo-Renaissance mansion on rue Tronchet, built for a Swiss banker and long one of the most tightly closed addresses in Paris. Today it hosts receptions and private parties.
summaries.Q3146003: Built in the eighteenth century for a banker's mistress, then passed to the Villeroy family. Since 1881 it has housed the Ministry of Agriculture, on rue de Varenne.
summaries.Q1643074: The house of the chaser Pierre Gouthière, eighteenth-century master of gilt bronze. He built it for himself, before his aristocratic clients ruined him by never paying their bills.
summaries.Q3145671: The mansion of the Paris branch of the Rothschilds, on rue Berryer, bequeathed to the State along with its collection. Its pavilion and grounds now host photography exhibitions.
summaries.Q3509682: An island of 6 700 m² on the lake of the Buttes-Chaumont, tied to the bank by a wooden footbridge to the west and by the stone pont des Suicidés to the south. At its summit, thirty metres above the water, stands the Temple of the Sibyl, a kiosk built in 1866 by Gabriel Davioud after the Temple of Vesta at Tivoli; its unstable foundations forced a complete rebuild in 1964.
summaries.Q3149058: The most exuberant Art nouveau façade in Paris, on avenue Rapp: flambé stoneware, sculpture and a doorway whose symbolism was so brazen it caused a scandal in 1901. It won its architect the city's prize for the finest façade.
summaries.Q3162463: Laid out from 1989 on the site of the old gare de Reuilly, this 15 200 m² garden turns around a broad, gently sloping semicircular lawn of 4 200 m², edged with small themed gardens and four statues picked from the City's storerooms. The passerelle André-Léo, by the architect Pierre Colboc, crosses it to carry the Promenade plantée.
summaries.Q3162555: A garden on the edge of the serres d'Auteuil, where lines of verse carved on steles walk along with you. Each grove is dedicated to a poet.
summaries.Q3162589: A botanical garden in the heart of the bois de Boulogne, with its Shakespeare garden growing the plants named in his plays. The name is said to come from a troubadour murdered here in the fourteenth century.
summaries.Q747835: On place Augusta-Holmes, a water dragon seems to burst from the ground three times over: two clear tubes curving in arcs, scaled along the top, where water races under high pressure in shifting light, and an opaque section emerging from the wall of an underground factory. Chen Zhen died in 2000 leaving the work at the sketch stage; his wife Xu Min completed it, unveiled in 2008.
summaries.Q3211300: The artists' café on rue de Seine, right among the Saint-Germain galleries. Its terrace and its 1930s ceramics make it one of the last genuine cafés in the quarter.
summaries.Q3218349: A restaurant founded in 1942 by René Lasserre, famous for its opening roof: in fine weather the dining room ceiling slides apart onto the Paris sky, mid-service.
summaries.Q3225157: A 1912 cinema that became, in 1978, the most sought-after nightclub in Paris, launched by Fabrice Emaer. Grace Jones, Karl Lagerfeld and Yves Saint Laurent turned it into the laboratory of Parisian nightlife.
summaries.Q1820520: The former refrigerated goods station of Paris-Ivry, squatted then made legal, now one of the biggest clusters of artists' studios in Paris. Its graffiti-covered walls stand out sharply against the new towers of the district.
summaries.Q3279717: Built in 1930 on rue Saint-Victor, the “Mutu” was the great amphitheatre of twentieth-century political rallies and trade-union congresses. Today it hosts events and concerts.
summaries.Q85854194: Set beneath place Denfert-Rochereau, in Colonel Rol-Tanguy's former command post during the liberation of Paris. You walk through the original underground HQ, twenty metres below street level.
summaries.Q642825: Three centuries of police history on the third floor of a working station house in the 5th arrondissement: prison registers, exhibits from crime scenes and famous cases, from Cartouche to Landru.
summaries.Q3330098: Founded in 1794 by René Just Haüy at the École des mines, a year after the Louvre and the Muséum, it is one of the oldest museums in France; it has occupied the hôtel de Vendôme, on boulevard Saint-Michel, since 1815. Of more than 100,000 specimens, 4,000 are on show in twelve rooms, among them cut gems from the Crown Jewels awarded to the school in 1887.
summaries.Q3364656: Created in 1977 on the edge of Issy-les-Moulineaux, between the Aquaboulevard and the heliport, this park is named after the tennis player Suzanne Lenglen. Its quirk: the football, rugby and athletics grounds are folded into a landscaped garden of winding paths and man-made hills, where an ecological pond also turns up.
summaries.Q2055785: Opened at the end of 1798, it owes its name to the Egyptian campaign led by Bonaparte, much in vogue in Paris at the time; three effigies of the goddess Hathor, recognisable by their cow ears, adorn its frontage on place du Caire. The oldest and longest covered arcade in Paris, 370 metres of glass roof, it was built over the Filles-Dieu convent, sold off as national property during the Revolution; the tombstones from its graveyard were then used as paving.
summaries.Q3367917: A discreet Marais alleyway, most of the time reserved for residents, running between rue Jean-Beausire and rue des Tournelles.
summaries.Q3367998: A private Marais passage that follows the line of Philip Augustus's old city wall. It is not open to the public.
summaries.Q2055779: An 1846 covered arcade extending the passage Jouffroy, under a glass roof on an iron frame. Secondhand booksellers, antiquarian dealers and old-photograph shops have made it their home.
summaries.Q3412678: The quay running along the Seine at the foot of the parc de Bercy and the finance ministry, out to the eastern edge of Paris.
summaries.Q3412685: Laid out in 1822 along with the canal Saint-Martin, this quay was first called quai Charles-X before taking the name of the battle of Jemmapes in 1830. At number 102, the Hôtel du Nord, where Eugène Dabit lived and worked for his hotel-keeper parents, inspired his 1928 novel, which Carné brought to the screen in 1938; declared unfit, it was saved when a demolition permit was refused in 1983.
summaries.Q3412716: The quay along the bassin de la Villette, between Ledoux's rotunda and the rue de Crimée lift bridge. Waterside bars and open-air cinema move in for the summer.
summaries.Q3427911: One of the oldest restaurants in Paris, housed in a pavilion in the Champs-Élysées gardens. Napoleon is said to have met Josephine here; the kitchen now holds three stars.
summaries.Q1496833: One of the oldest streets on the Left Bank: its name appears as early as 1247, borrowed from a shop sign showing King David holding a harp. Before that it was the Vieille-Boucherie, then the Bouclerie, after the craftsmen who worked there. It cut through the heart of the medieval university and served a whole string of colleges (Harcourt, Cluny, Narbonne, Bayeux) of which almost nothing survives: the cutting of boulevard Saint-Michel swallowed most of it.
summaries.Q3451451: A medieval lane in the Latin Quarter, facing Notre-Dame, named after a shop sign recorded in the late thirteenth century, La Huchette d'or. Now almost entirely pedestrian, it has one of the highest concentrations of restaurants in Paris, among them many Greek tavernas. At number 23 hides the Théâtre de la Huchette, which has been playing the same two Ionesco plays without a break since 1957.
summaries.Q3450806: The bal-musette street. It owes its name to Gérard de Lappe, a market gardener who grew his crops here in the seventeenth century, and was briefly called rue Louis-Philippe after the king's visit in 1830. In the nineteenth century it was colonised by Auvergnats who had come up to Paris as wood and coal merchants and opened the dance halls where the accordion dethroned the cabrette bagpipe. The Balajo, opened in 1936, keeps the tradition alive; the rest of the street has become the heart of Bastille nightlife.
summaries.Q3451675: A Marais street whose name tells the story of a garment: the monks of the order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin, settled there in 1258, wore a white cloak. Before them it was rue de la Parcheminerie, after the workshops where skins were prepared for writing. The present name was fixed around 1289 and appears in Guillot's Dit des rues de Paris, around 1300. The Blancs-Manteaux church, rebuilt in the seventeenth century, keeps a Flemish marquetry pulpit given to it in the nineteenth.
summaries.Q3469893: Probably the oldest party venue still standing in Paris, and the last relic of the great nineteenth-century ballrooms. It all began after Waterloo with the bal Dourlans, an open-air tavern opened by a veteran of the Imperial Guard just outside the Farmers-General wall, where wine escaped the city toll. Renamed salle Wagram, it has hosted popular dances, political meetings and boxing matches, then concerts and recording sessions; its gilded-balcony hall now serves the studios as much as the parties.
summaries.Q3494878: A private estate hidden behind a carriage arch on rue Taitbout, built from 1829 by the English architect Edward Cresy on the model of London squares: six neoclassical buildings around two cobbled courtyards and a fountain. It was first called cité des Trois-Frères. In the 1840s Frédéric Chopin lodged at number 9 and George Sand at number 5, a few metres apart, with Alexandre Dumas and the dancer Marie Taglioni for neighbours.
summaries.Q3494691: The terraced garden climbing towards the Sacré-Cœur, laid out in the late nineteenth century to dress the 23,000 m2 of hillside. Horseshoe ramps, slanting staircases and Paul Gasq's big fountain organise the ascent; the funicular, running since 1900, hugs the whole western side. Renamed in 2004 after the Communard Louise Michel, a Montmartre schoolteacher, it is now one of the most visited free sites in France.
summaries.Q3390093: A sunken, quiet garden on the north slope of the butte, away from the Sacré-Cœur crowds. A statue of Saint Denis stands above a waterless fountain: the spring, said to be the one where the first bishop of Paris, beheaded in the third century, washed his severed head before walking on, dried up in 1810 after an underground collapse. Since 1954 the square has carried the name of Suzanne Buisson, a socialist Resistance member who died at Auschwitz.
summaries.Q2895806: Under the chestnut trees of the Champs-Élysées, this address has led one life after another since 1772: the café des Ambassadeurs licensed under Louis XV, a café-concert where Mistinguett and Yvette Guilbert sang, the théâtre des Ambassadeurs, then the espace Pierre-Cardin from 1970 to 2016. The City of Paris reopened it in March 2024 as the théâtre de la Concorde, with a 673-seat main hall, a cinema and a programme built around democratic debate.
summaries.Q3496252: The second stage of the Théâtre de la Ville, opened in 1996 at the foot of the butte, on the site of a cluster of butcher's shops including the famous Cochon Rose. The Belgian architect Charles Vandenhove chose a neoclassical postmodernism rare in France, while meeting an unusual condition: to block nothing of the view up to the Bateau-Lavoir, higher on the hill. The proscenium curtain and the galleries were painted by Olivier Debré.
summaries.Q3527758: An Italian-style house of 386 seats, opened in 1898, named after the Mathurin order that owned a garden here from 1246. In the 1930s Georges Pitoëff and his wife Ludmilla turned it into a laboratory of modern staging, introducing Chekhov, Pirandello and Ibsen to Parisian audiences. The neighbourhood keeps a darker memory: the cemetery next door, opened in 1721, took in the 133 people suffocated at the fireworks for Louis XVI's wedding, and later the bodies of the king and Marie-Antoinette.
summaries.Q3434524: A rotunda built in 1860 by Gabriel Davioud for the Panorama National: visitors stood at the centre of canvases 14 metres high and 120 round, depicting Sevastopol or Solferino. It became the Palais de Glace in 1893, a fashionable ice rink into the 1970s, and has been a theatre since 1981 under Renaud-Barrault, then a house for living playwrights under Jean-Michel Ribes, who left at the end of 2022.
summaries.Q3527562: A 498-seat private theatre opened in 1929, built by Camille Choisy, former boss of the Grand-Guignol, with architect Charles Siclis. The work was so rushed that an actor in the opening play claimed the staircase swallowed three quarters of the available space, and that someone realised at the last minute it might be wise to allow for a stage as well. It became a temple of boulevard comedy and launched dozens of hits under the Deutsch family's management.
summaries.Q3558850: A private cul-de-sac in the 18th arrondissement holding the largest set of 19th-century artists' studios in Paris: some fifty of them, built in 1888 by architect Henri Cambon on land carved off the Montmartre cemetery. The main staircase and several other elements were salvaged from pavilions of the 1900 Universal Exhibition. Cézanne, Signac, Dufy, Le Douanier Rousseau, Picabia and Eugène Carrière all worked here; the complex has been a listed historic monument since 1994.
summaries.Q17376345: Anne of Austria had vowed to raise a « magnificent temple » if God gave her a son: Louis-Dieudonné was born in 1638 and, aged seven, laid the church's first stone himself in 1645. Mansart, Lemercier, Le Muet and finally Le Duc completed it in 1667. The chapel of hearts held the embalmed hearts of 45 kings and queens; during the Revolution, thirteen urns were sold to painters, who cooked them down into a glaze.
summaries.Q4724424: A music hall opened in 1904 at 50 rue de Malte and pulled down in 1967; the new Alhambra opened in April 2008 on rue Yves-Toudic, three hundred metres away. Rebuilt after the fire of 1925, the old house had gold-leaf stucco that earned it the nickname « the gilded temple »; it was here, in 1936, that la Môme Piaf, 19 years old, was pushed on stage for the first time.
summaries.Q2859130: The big water park of Paris, opened in 1989 on six hectares built over the ring road, in the 15th arrondissement. Under a 7 000 m2 glass roof planted with palm trees, the Aqua Park lines up slides, artificial waves and a lagoon kept at 29 degrees all year round. The complex also holds a gym, tennis and squash courts and a fourteen-screen cinema.
summaries.Q2973092: Built in 1878 in old quarries under the hill of Chaillot, it is the world's first aquarium; closed in 1985 because it had fallen into disrepair, it reopened in 2006. Its main tank holds 38 sharks of seven species. Before that, these galleries stabled Napoleon's cavalry, and the mix of straw and manure got the growing of the Paris mushroom started.
summaries.Q2932275: A permanent big top pitched in the parc de la Villette, created in 1997 by Méziane Azaïche to give world music a stage, from raï to gnawa by way of jazz and hip-hop. The room seats 600, or takes 1 200 standing. In 2019 the old tent was replaced by an all-timber structure designed by Dutch architect Boris Zeisser.
summaries.Q2932969: On the place de l'Odéon, one of the busiest literary cafés of the 19th century. Delacroix lunched here in 1824, Balzac put it into Les Martyrs ignorés, and the regulars answered to Verlaine, Mallarmé, Gauguin or Barrès. Next door stood the home of Camille and Lucile Desmoulins, arrested there in 1793. The café is gone: the address now houses the literature department of the Flammarion publishing house.
summaries.Q38941403: A monastery of cloistered Carmelite nuns at the foot of the Sacré-Cœur bell tower, on rue du Chevalier-de-la-Barre. The community follows the rule reformed by St Teresa of Ávila in the 16th century: silence, prayer and manual work, a few metres from the stream of visitors flooding the Butte. From the street you see nothing but the wall and a discreet door.
summaries.Q2944288: A 39 000 m2 arts venue set in the former municipal undertakers of Paris, built in 1874 under Victor Baltard in the manner of an industrial market hall, glass roofs and iron frames included. Until 1993, almost every funeral procession in the city set off from here. Reopened in 2008 as an arts factory, the Centquatre leaves its naves open free of charge: dancers, jugglers and circus performers come and rehearse there all day long.
summaries.Q2957470: The Père-Lachaise chapel stands on top of Mont-Louis, on the exact spot of the Jesuit rest house where Father La Chaise, Louis XIV's confessor, used to come and recover; the cemetery took his name. Built in 1823 and facing east, it commands the whole site, in line with the main entrance. It opens to the public only on 1 and 2 November; Adolphe Thiers's monumental tomb sits right beside it.
summaries.Q2956622: The chapel of the Picpus cemetery, one of only two private cemeteries in Paris. In two mass graves the ground received the bodies of 1 306 people guillotined on the place du Trône-Renversé during the six weeks of the Great Terror, in 1794. Families of the victims bought the site back to keep its memory alive; La Fayette lies here under an American flag renewed every 4 July.
summaries.Q2956625: The last church built in France in the 20th century. Designed by Pierre-Louis Faloci in the heart of the new Paris Rive Gauche district, it was finished in 2000 after a delay caused by a crane collapsing during the storm of December 1999. Bare concrete volumes, light from above and not a scrap of ornament: the building was given the 20th-century heritage label as early as 2011.
summaries.Q54002491: A chapel sunk below rue d'Auteuil, reached down a flight of steps. The land belonged to Pierre Chardon, known as the doctor of the poor; his son made a fortune there and opened next door the old people's home that became the Chardon-Lagache hospital. In 1953 architect Raymond Busse hid the whole thing behind a bell-tower façade aligned with the neighbouring blocks, which makes it almost invisible from the street.
summaries.Q2957104: Commissioned in 1909 by Marie de la Passion just after Joan of Arc's beatification and blessed in 1913: a reinforced-concrete chapel in a neo-Gothic style drawn from the Sainte-Chapelle. Its stained glass forms an itinerary, each window carrying the name and the date of a town Joan passed through; the chancel window shows her entering Orléans on 8 May 1429.
summaries.Q1094315: A village inside the city: a private lane 320 metres long, opened in 1847 in the Épinettes quarter, lined with middle-class houses whose façades are all different and with small gardens spilling over with climbing plants. Two very strict founding covenants froze its character and blocked any rebuilding into apartment blocks. The public is tolerated there from 7:00 to 19:00 on weekdays.
summaries.Q2974812: Twenty-nine white half-timbered chalets behind a gate on boulevard Arago. The first building, in 1878, was put together with materials from the Food pavilion of the Universal Exhibition; the second followed in 1888. Modigliani had his studio here, Rodin and Maillol had their bronzes patinated here. Targeted by a property scheme, the cité was saved in 1974 by its own residents.
summaries.Q2974809: A triangle of low houses and flowery alleys in the south of the 13th arrondissement, built in 1928. The ground, a former meadow regularly flooded by the Bièvre, was too soft to carry apartment blocks: only small houses went up. The streets are named after flowers (des Glycines, des Iris, des Volubilis) and the residents have buried the façades under climbing roses.
summaries.Q22248248: The largest artists' complex in Europe: 180 studio-flats put up in the 1930s on rue Ordener at the instigation of sculptor Louis-Aimé Lejeune. The idea was to offer artists studio space at low rent, just as property speculation was driving them out of Montmartre. Still run by the city's social housing landlord, it shelters painters, sculptors and engravers behind brick façades pierced by big north-facing windows.
summaries.Q3494303: A neighbourhood church opened in 1957 on rue Lecourbe, run by the Religious of Saint Vincent de Paul, settled there since 1935 to look after the working-class youth of the 15th arrondissement. Sober post-war architecture, restored in 2001, with an organ that Paris organists hold in high regard.
summaries.Q3584716: Consecrated in 1968, it rests on a steel frame sheathed entirely in aluminium sheets, inside and out, and its metal tower carries bells and cross 35 metres up. The metal answers to Saint Eligius, patron of goldsmiths and metalworkers; the light, for its part, falls from glass panels slipped in a staggered pattern between the metal ones, without its source ever showing.
summaries.Q3076004: Built in 1715-1717 to bring drinking water to the Saint-Germain-des-Prés quarter, it had a twin facing it on the corner of rue Childebert, a street wiped out in 1867 when rue de Rennes was cut through. Re-erected in 1875 in square Paul-Langevin against the wall of the old École polytechnique, it pours its water through a bronze mascaron; its sister is in storage at the musée Carnavalet.
summaries.Q3076018: A fountain from 1840, facing the Jardin des plantes, in tribute to Georges Cuvier, founder of palaeontology. An allegory of natural history bears his motto, Rerum cognoscere causas, surrounded by sea creatures and amphibians. Naturalists in the quarter have always relished one detail: the sculpted crocodile turns its neck at a right angle, a movement the animal is anatomically incapable of.
summaries.Q3076204: A fountain planted on the central island of the faubourg Saint-Antoine, opposite the Saint-Antoine hospital. Its name comes from the small covered market built in 1643 by the abbess of Saint-Antoine-des-Champs, who held the monopoly on selling meat in the faubourg. Back then the spot marked the fork where the roads to Vincennes and Montreuil parted, right in the heart of the cabinetmakers' quarter.
summaries.Q3076301: This 1906 fountain marks the site of the first artesian well in Paris. From 1833 to 1841, engineer Louis-Georges Mulot, backed by the astronomer François Arago, drilled for eight years before striking water at 548 metres down, which made it the deepest borehole in the world. The water then gushed into a 42-metre metal tower standing on place de Breteuil, demolished in 1903.
summaries.Q16638401: The Muséum's herbarium, the largest in the world: nearly eight million dried plant specimens housed in the south building of the Jardin des plantes, 5.8 million of them already digitised. Among them are 500,000 type specimens, the ones that served as the model for a species' scientific description and stand as the reference for the international community. The collections go back to the herbaria of Tournefort and Lamarck.
summaries.Q1543030: Opened in 1856 on rue de Clignancourt, this working-class department store sold furniture and household goods on credit: a collector called on borrowers every week, and borrowers were only accepted after the concierges had been quizzed about them. By 1912 it employed 15,000 people. Its 47.50-metre dome, topped with an electric beacon to guide customers in, was demolished in 1957; the pediment carved by Dalou survives.
summaries.Q3145392: The only surviving building by Étienne-Louis Boullée, the visionary architect of giant cenotaphs and impossible spheres, who built almost nothing he drew. Erected from 1763 to 1766 for a councillor at the Cour des aides, this early work recalls the Petit Trianon: columns on the courtyard side, a colossal order facing the garden. It later belonged to Marshal Suchet.
summaries.Q15950560: A rental block built around 1728 by the Carmelites of the neighbouring monastery, who were letting out part of their land. Chateaubriand lived here from 1825 to 1826, between two ambassadorships, and Marshal Victor after him. The house lost its garden around 1908 when the boulevard Raspail was cut through, slicing the plot in two.
summaries.Q1952743: Built from 1776 to 1792 for the Marquis de Galliffet and seized as émigré property, it became the Ministry of Foreign Relations in 1794. Talleyrand moved in in 1797, and it was here, on 3 January 1798, that he introduced Bonaparte to Madame de Staël. Italy leased it in 1894 and bought it in 1909; today it houses the Italian Cultural Institute.
summaries.Q3145894: Built from 1777 to 1779 on the Champs-Élysées and threatened with demolition in 1927, it was moved stone by stone to a corner of the Observatoire garden to house the Société des gens de lettres. In 1870 the Duke of Massa had closed its shutters at the sight of German troops marching past, swearing to open them only on the day of revenge; his nephew opened them on 14 July 1919, and closed them again on the 15th.
summaries.Q3145893: Built in 1787 by Alexandre-Théodore Brongniart, the future architect of the Bourse, for Prince Masserano, a grandee of Spain from the Genoese house of Fieschi. It is one of the last aristocratic commissions in the Invalides district before the Revolution, in the most stripped-down neoclassical taste. The street itself is named after the man who ordered it.
summaries.Q3145918: The Comte de Montmorin, later foreign minister to Louis XVI, bought this house on rue Oudinot in 1784, raised on ground that was half marsh; accused of aiding the flight to Varennes, he was killed in the massacres of September 1792. After half a century of the Brothers of the Christian Schools, the City traded it to the State in 1906 for a barracks, and the Ministry of the Colonies moved in.
summaries.Q1643125: A house of 1780 by the architect Nicolas-Claude Girardin, mentioned by Chateaubriand in the Mémoires d'outre-tombe. It was bought by the Countess Merlin, a Cuban born Mercedes de Santa Cruz, who ran one of the most sought-after salons of romantic Paris here: George Sand, Balzac, Musset, Mérimée and Rossini all came to hear her sing. The street façade and roof are listed historic monuments.
summaries.Q3145567: An Art Deco villa of 1927, built on avenue Junot for the sculptor Louis-Aimé Lejeune, the very man who would have the cité Montmartre-aux-artistes put up a few years later. The avenue, cut through in 1910 across the old maquis of Montmartre, is packed with artists' houses from between the wars. Façades and roofs have been listed historic monuments since 1982.
summaries.Q3145634: A private palace in the French classical style, raised from 1878 to 1884 for the Polish count Mikołaj Potocki, with a cour d'honneur, stables and a monumental double-revolution grand staircase that ranks among the most spectacular in Paris. The Paris chamber of commerce occupied it for close to a century; major works began in 2025 to bring in company headquarters.
summaries.Q3510125: A two-hectare artificial island, born with Lake Daumesnil when the bois de Vincennes was laid out. Bean-shaped, it can only be reached by a suspension bridge some twenty metres long, and even then: it leads to the île de Reuilly, the only one linked to the shore. A plane tree planted in 1860 rises 45 metres here.
summaries.Q3510089: The larger of the two islands in Lake Daumesnil, at 2.5 hectares, and the more surprising: it holds a neoclassical temple perched on an artificial rock, a grotto and a waterfall, the romantic scenery typical of Second Empire gardens. The rock was built from the stone dug out to make the lake. Two small suspension bridges lead across.
summaries.Q103456427: This Montmartre cabaret opened in 1908 at the corner of rue des Saules and rue de l'Abreuvoir, created by the dancer Germaine Pichot and her husband, the Catalan painter Ramon Pichot. Close to Picasso and his circle, she had been loved by the painter Carles Casagemas, who took his own life in 1901. Modigliani, Camus, Piaf and Brel all passed through; Utrillo painted it, and tourism has made it one of the most photographed spots in Paris.
summaries.Q6488471: A restaurant on quai des Grands-Augustins set in a private mansion from the end of Louis XIV's reign, turned wine merchant's shop in 1766. Its little private rooms with locking doors made its legend: ladies checked whether the diamonds they were given were real by scratching them on the mirrors, and the marks are still there. Hugo, Zola, Maupassant, Colette and Proust all dined here.
summaries.Q3233951: France's oldest LGBT bookshop, opened in 1980 on rue Simart. The name comes from its beginnings: bookshop by day, tea room and restaurant by night, a gastro-literary blend that lasted only a few months but left its sign behind. For thirty-five years it stood on rue Sainte-Croix-de-la-Bretonnerie, where it helped turn the Marais into a gay neighbourhood, before moving to rue Saint-Ambroise in 2020.
summaries.Q133105556: The bookshop of the Fédération anarchiste, founded on 18 March 1959, a date picked for the anniversary of the Paris Commune. With La Gryffe in Lyon, it is one of France's two historic libertarian bookshops: it publishes, prints and distributes, and houses the studios of Radio libertaire. On rue Amelot since 1981.
summaries.Q3278492: Built from 1888 to 1892 by Marcellin Varcollier on place Jules-Joffrin, on the site of the Clignancourt farm that belonged to the abbey of Montmartre. It replaced the old town hall of the commune of Montmartre on place des Abbesses, whose grounds became square Jehan-Rictus. In July 1942 one of its rooms served as an assembly point for Jews during the Vél d'Hiv roundup.
summaries.Q1033700: Set up in 1946 to thank the Latin American nations for their support during the war, the Maison de l'Amérique latine has occupied two mansions on boulevard Saint-Germain since 1965, the hôtels Amelot de Gournay and de Varengeville. It hosts exhibitions, talks and concerts, and its 1,000 m2 garden is one of the few private green spaces open to the public in the faubourg Saint-Germain.
summaries.Q3279689: A mansion on rue Saint-Dominique, home to the La Tour d'Auvergne, Caraman and La Rochefoucauld d'Estissac families until 1929, then turned into a conference centre inaugurated on 1 December 1934 in the presence of President Albert Lebrun. In December 1935 it was one of six places in Paris to carry the very first public television broadcast in France.
summaries.Q22922153: Le Corbusier's first Paris house, built from 1922 to 1924 with Pierre Jeanneret for the painter Amédée Ozenfant, his co-founder of purism. It applies the principles the architect would only later set down in theory: bare volumes, an external spiral staircase and above all a studio on the second floor lit by a sawtooth corner skylight borrowed from factories. The original roof was replaced in 1946.
summaries.Q3289864: Open every morning except Monday, it comes in two halves: the covered Beauvau hall, built in 1779 on land bought from the nuns of Saint-Antoine and rebuilt in 1843, and the open-air market on the square, where the second-hand dealers hold the eastern half-circle. The two names come from a first president of the Parlement de Paris and from the last abbess of Saint-Antoine-des-Champs.
summaries.Q3323366: A six-metre statue standing on the esplanade d'Arménie, between the pont des Invalides and the Grand Palais, in memory of the victims of the 1915 genocide and of the Armenian fighters who died for France. It portrays Komitas, a priest and musicologist who collected thousands of Armenian folk songs and sank into silence after surviving the deportations. The project was voted on 29 January 2001, the day France recognised the genocide.
summaries.Q3323309: The great sculpted wall that closes the vista of the main avenue at Père-Lachaise, the work of Paul-Albert Bartholomé, unveiled in 1899 after twelve years' labour. It shows an anonymous crowd advancing towards a dark doorway and, below, a couple lying in the earth: a monument to all the dead, whatever their religion or rank, which was a bold move at the time. An ossuary was dug beneath the hill in the 1950s.
summaries.Q17745972: A bas-relief in the jardin d'agronomie tropicale, in the bois de Vincennes, honouring the tirailleurs who came from Africa and died for France. The sculptor Auguste Biaggi shows a barefoot widow before a grave figured by a poilu's helmet set on a stake. Unlike the neighbouring monument to Madagascan soldiers, its unveiling seems to have left no trace at all in the press of the day.
summaries.Q24931083: A museum devoted entirely to language and linguistics, opened in 2013 by Mark Oremland, a New Zealander who came to Paris to study the subject. Across two floors and 170 m2 it gathers a thousand objects and hands-on displays: a Braille typewriter, recordings of whistled languages, translation games. A rare curiosity, a stone's throw from the Luxembourg Gardens.
summaries.Q3330333: A private museum on the history of chocolate, opened in 2010 on boulevard de Bonne-Nouvelle, on the site of a former dance hall. A thousand or so objects trace cocoa's journey from the Maya, who drank it bitter and peppered, to the industrial bar. A chocolatier gives moulding demonstrations on the spot.
summaries.Q3330353: A small private museum founded in 2001 to document the act of smoking and the plants people smoke, neither preaching nor promoting. On show: clay pipes, opium pipes, hookahs, peace pipes, snuffboxes and old botanical plates. An unlikely collection, a stone's throw from rue de la Roquette.
summaries.Q657624: Paris's benchmark jazz club, opened on 16 April 1981 by Eglal Farhi in the former print works of Le Parisien. Art Blakey and his Jazz Messengers played the opening night. Since then the 500-seat room has seen Chet Baker, Dizzy Gillespie, Stan Getz, B. B. King and, one July night in 2010, Prince in a surprise gig.
summaries.Q3361052: A monumental building of 630 rooms, put up in 1910 to house single male workers thanks to the discreet backing of the philanthropist Amicie Lebaudy. Since 1641 the plot had belonged to a Dominican convent said to hold the grave of Cyrano de Bergerac. The Salvation Army bought it in 1926 and opened it to women on their own, hence the name; it is now one of the largest shelters in Paris.
summaries.Q3364156: A sloping garden that runs down the hill of Passy to the Seine, opened in 2004 on ground long cluttered with government prefabs. Its long walk of flowering arches sits on the site of the Eaux de Passy: a spring found around 1657, a spa opened in 1720, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau writing Le Devin du village here.
summaries.Q3363907: A rolling six-hectare park in Auteuil, once the estate of the abbey of Sainte-Geneviève, which had been sending its monks here for country rest since 1109. Sold off as national property during the Revolution, it was bought back for the institution Sainte-Périne, a retirement home turned hospital that still lines its edge. Ancient trees and sloping lawns make it one of the quietest gardens in the 16th.
summaries.Q76350559: Opened in November 2018 in front of the Hospitalières-Saint-Gervais primary school, this forecourt bears the number of its Jewish pupils deported in the Vél d'Hiv roundup of 16 and 17 July 1942 and then murdered in the camps. A plaque at the school entrance records their names.
summaries.Q636538: Formerly ruelle Mazagran, renamed in 1877, it long vied with rue du Chat-qui-Pêche and sentier des Merisiers for the title of narrowest street in Paris, at 80 centimetres across. A rebuild in the 2000s widened it to several metres, steps included. “Duée” is an old word for a gushing spring.
summaries.Q3368085: A passage cut in 1699 under the name rue Abbatiale, inside the precinct of the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Its name recalls the old rue des Boucheries, swallowed when boulevard Saint-Germain was driven through, where meat stalls spilled onto jutting boards under wooden awnings. Today it comes out just behind the church's bell tower.
summaries.Q3367986: A quiet covered passage linking rue Saint-Paul to the side door of the church of Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis. It once served the hôtel de Damville, home of Madeleine de Savoie, widow of the Constable Anne de Montmorency, whose grounds reached as far as rue Saint-Antoine. The Cardinal de Bourbon handed it to the Jesuits in 1580, and they built their chapel there.
summaries.Q3368001: A passage that hugs the exact outline of the church of Sainte-Élisabeth, between rue du Temple and rue de Turbigo. That curving line is the fossil of the old precinct of the convent of the Filles de Sainte-Élisabeth, founded in 1616 by Marie de' Medici, of which the church is the only surviving trace.
summaries.Q16510070: A 1.2-kilometre linear park on the old Auteuil line, opened in 1854 by the Pereire brothers and later folded into the Petite Ceinture. Closed in 1985, the cutting turned into wasteland where buddleias and elders seeded themselves, before opening to the public in 2007. The rails are gone, apart from one stub at the rue du Ranelagh entrance; the ballast, though, stayed put.
summaries.Q3389213: The pool of the 1924 Olympic Games, the ones where Johnny Weissmuller, the future Tarzan, took three titles. Long the home of the French swimming federation, it has borne the name of Georges Vallerey, a swimmer who died at 27, since 1959. Its 50-metre basin sits under a retractable roof: in fine weather you swim under open sky. It served as a training pool for the 2024 Games.
